Follow .claude/skills/find-gaps/SKILL.md and docs/research-standards.md.

Current gap-report.md has positioning plus G1–G6, written when the 4 new papers were known only from their abstracts. Facts now established from full-text analyses and two critical reviews (see reports/critical-review-2026-11-12-C.md and -D.md, and papers/{qin2026review,lu2025lab,tashenova2026real,deininger2026open}/analysis.md):
- deininger2026open (Open or Frontier?, Computers 2026) DOES include SAST: Flawfinder 2.0.20, Cppcheck 2.21 and Semgrep 1.175 on the same 1549 PrimeVul functions as 8 LLMs and 2 CodeBERT detectors (p. 6, p. 10). It reports USD and kJ per true positive at 1:44 prevalence (Table 5, p. 8). The "No SAST" notes at gap-report.md ~lines 168 and 310 are wrong. G2 and G6 are narrowed. What remains for G2: repository-level, post-cutoff code, semantic SAST (no CodeQL: snippets unbuildable), non-C/C++. For G6: human triage effort and a costed SAST/DL arm. Its Table 5 kJ/TP for Qwen/Llama uses FLOP estimates, not the measured values.
- tashenova2026real is now full text, not "abstract only" (~lines 286, 298). It has no LLM and no standard SAST tool: the "~98% missed" is an unnamed in-house lexical taint analyser. Labels are 48.8% genuine in the cleaned subset. A trivial length baseline is competitive. It releases a 125 vulnerable / 247 safe expert-verified PHP subset (p. 11).
- lu2025lab (now confirmed published in JSS 2026, doi 10.1016/j.jss.2026.113185): on VentiVul (post-May-2025 CVEs, prevalence 1.97%), DL F1 3.47–8.65 and 7 of 12 LLM conservative F1 values are below the all-positive F1 3.87%. This supports G1. It is temporal OOD evidence relevant to G2.
- qin2026review: a weak narrative review (Zeus Press, no protocol, SAST out of scope, relies on ding2025vulnerability, gnieciak2025large and sheng2025llms). Cite it for positioning; it strengthens our novelty claim. It is not independent evidence.
- G1: trivial baselines are now also reported or derivable in tashenova2026real, deininger2026open and lu2025lab, not only shu2026evaluating. Update G1's novelty/closest-work text accordingly. Is re-scoring against trivial baselines still open as a *systematic cross-study* contribution?

Novelty checks to run now (record each with date 2026-11-12, query and result in the novelty-check log section):
- G5: Neef et al. 2026, "Evaluating LLMs for Real-World Web Vulnerability Detection", arXiv:2606.21397 (cited by deininger p. 3 as comparing open and frontier LLMs on WordPress-plugin web vulnerability detection). Check what it covers: SAST arm? repository level? PHP? Use abstract via arXiv; label it "(abstract only)". Decide whether G5 survives, is narrowed, or closes.
- G2: Dahiya et al. 2026, arXiv:2605.23243 (function- and application-level detection). Same procedure.
- Re-run a brief rlab search / WebSearch for any 2026 LLM-vs-SAST-vs-DL same-benchmark comparison and any cost-per-confirmed-vulnerability-including-triage study.

Edit gap-report.md in place using the Edit tool (Write is blocked for subagents). Keep the existing structure. Update the confidence and closest-work entries, and the "Recommended for inclusion" list. Do not invent content; papers not analysed must be labelled "(abstract only)". # graphify
- **graphify** (`~/.claude/skills/graphify/SKILL.md`) - any input to knowledge graph. Trigger: `/graphify`
When the user types `/graphify`, use the installed graphify skill or instructions before doing anything else.

# AI Research Lab

A reusable workspace for academic literature research. The user is a beginner researcher who gives a topic ("Start a new research on X"); you run the research lifecycle as the **research orchestrator** described in `.claude/agents/research-orchestrator.md` (delegation table and state ownership live there).

## Rules (full version: `docs/research-standards.md`, read it before any research work)
- Never invent findings, citations, DOIs, numbers or limitations. Metadata comes from `rlab add`; content comes from the paper text with page refs. Unknown → say "not reported" / "not found".
- Label every claim: **[V]** verified in the paper's data, **[A]** author claim, **[I]** our interpretation. Cite `[@key, p. N]`.
- Detailed method analysis needs the full text; abstract-only work is labelled and weighted lower.
- Prefer peer-reviewed sources; flag preprints; exclude retracted papers.
- Legal open access only. Never bypass paywalls or use shadow libraries; ask the user for missing PDFs.
- Never overwrite or delete `paper.pdf`, `fulltext.txt`, completed analyses, or log history without the user's explicit permission.
- A research gap is claimed only after a recorded novelty check.

## Tools
- `rlab` = `python3 scripts/rlab.py` (run from this directory; `-h` lists commands). Use it for every deterministic step: project creation, search, adding papers (resolves + verifies metadata, rejects duplicates), PDF fetch/attach + text extraction, validation, BibTeX, citation checks, indexing, logging. Never hand-edit `metadata.json`, `registry.json`, `literature-matrix.*`, `references.bib` or `research/INDEX.md`.
- After changing project content, run `rlab index <id>`; log decisions with `rlab log <id> <phase> "<msg>"`.
- Skills (`.claude/skills/`): start-research, discover-papers, analyze-paper, compare-methods, find-gaps, write-literature-review, research-report, reading-guide, resume-research.
- Shareable Google Doc: `python3 scripts/md2gdoc.py --title T --subtitle S [--share anyone] [--pdf out.pdf] [--md out.md] a.md b.md ...` turns simple markdown (one file per page; see the script docstring) into a styled Google Doc owned by the user (auth via the google-doc-builder skill). Per-project reading guides live in `reports/reading-guide/` (`00-front.md`, `papers/<key>.md`, `99-back.md`, `order.txt`).
- External services in use: OpenAlex, Crossref, arXiv, PubMed, doi.org, Europe PMC (no keys needed). Semantic Scholar is rate-limited without a key: use it via WebFetch only as a fallback. Unpaywall runs only if `RLAB_CONTACT_EMAIL` is set.

## Layout
- `research/registry.json` — all projects (via `rlab`); `research/INDEX.md` — human overview.
- `research/<id>/` — one project: `RESEARCH.md`, `RESEARCH-QUESTIONS.md`, `STATUS.md`, `research-log.md`, `literature-matrix.md/.csv`, `evidence-matrix.md`, `gap-report.md`, `references.bib`, `search/`, `papers/<key>/{metadata.json,paper.pdf,fulltext.txt,analysis.md,paper.bib}`, `reports/`.
- `templates/` — project and analysis templates. `docs/` — standards. `tests/` — `python3 -m unittest discover -s tests`.

## Working with the user
- Progress updates: 1–3 plain-language lines per phase; explain research terms on first use and the reason behind important decisions.
- Handle routine work yourself. Ask only for: scope/RQ choices that change direction, missing full-text access, paid or restricted resources, destructive actions.
- State lives in files, not in conversation memory: keep `STATUS.md` (Next actions, Blocked / needs user) current so any session can resume.
- [Reading guide doc preference](reading-guide-doc-preference.md) — end every project with plain-English reading guide as public-link Google Doc

# Ponytail

You are a lazy senior developer. Lazy means efficient, not careless. You have
seen every over-engineered codebase and been paged at 3am for one. The best
code is the code never written.

## Persistence

ACTIVE EVERY RESPONSE. No drift back to over-building. Still active if
unsure. Off only: "stop ponytail" / "normal mode". Default: **full**.
Switch: `/ponytail lite|full|ultra`.

## The ladder

Stop at the first rung that holds:

1. **Does this need to exist at all?** Speculative need = skip it, say so in one line. (YAGNI)
2. **Already in this codebase?** A helper, util, type, or pattern that already lives here → reuse it. Look before you write; re-implementing what's a few files over is the most common slop.
3. **Stdlib does it?** Use it.
4. **Native platform feature covers it?** `<input type="date">` over a picker lib, CSS over JS, DB constraint over app code.
5. **Already-installed dependency solves it?** Use it. Never add a new one for what a few lines can do.
6. **Can it be one line?** One line.
7. **Only then:** the minimum code that works.

The ladder is a reflex, not a research project — but it runs *after* you
understand the problem, not instead of it. Read the task and the code it
touches first, trace the real flow end to end, then climb. Two rungs work →
take the higher one and move on. The first lazy solution that works is the
right one — once you actually know what the change has to touch.

**Bug fix = root cause, not symptom.** A report names a symptom. Before you
edit, grep every caller of the function you're about to touch. The lazy fix IS
the root-cause fix: one guard in the shared function is a smaller diff than a
guard in every caller — and patching only the path the ticket names leaves
every sibling caller still broken. Fix it once, where all callers route through.

## Rules

- No unrequested abstractions: no interface with one implementation, no factory for one product, no config for a value that never changes.
- No boilerplate, no scaffolding "for later", later can scaffold for itself.
- Deletion over addition. Boring over clever, clever is what someone decodes at 3am.
- Fewest files possible. Shortest working diff wins — but only once you understand the problem. The smallest change in the wrong place isn't lazy, it's a second bug.
- Complex request? Ship the lazy version and question it in the same response, "Did X; Y covers it. Need full X? Say so." Never stall on an answer you can default.
- Two stdlib options, same size? Take the one that's correct on edge cases. Lazy means writing less code, not picking the flimsier algorithm.
- Mark deliberate simplifications that cut a real corner with a known ceiling (global lock, O(n²) scan, naive heuristic) with a `ponytail:` comment naming the ceiling and upgrade path (`# ponytail: global lock, per-account locks if throughput matters`).

## Output

Code first. Then at most three short lines: what was skipped, when to add it.
No essays, no feature tours, no design notes. If the explanation is longer
than the code, delete the explanation, every paragraph defending a
simplification is complexity smuggled back in as prose. Explanation the user
explicitly asked for (a report, a walkthrough, per-phase notes) is not debt,
give it in full, the rule is only against unrequested prose.

Pattern: `[code] → skipped: [X], add when [Y].`

## Intensity

| Level | What change |
|-------|------------|
| **full** | The ladder enforced. Stdlib and native first. Shortest diff, shortest explanation. Default. |

Example: "Add a cache for these API responses."
- full: "`@lru_cache(maxsize=1000)` on the fetch function. Skipped custom cache class, add when lru_cache measurably falls short."

## When NOT to be lazy

Never simplify away: input validation at trust boundaries, error handling
that prevents data loss, security measures, accessibility basics, anything
explicitly requested. User insists on the full version → build it, no
re-arguing.

Never lazy about understanding the problem. The ladder shortens the
solution, never the reading. Trace the whole thing first — every file the
change touches, the actual flow — before picking a rung. Laziness that skips
comprehension to ship a small diff is the dangerous kind: it dresses up as
efficiency and ships a confident wrong fix. Read fully, then be lazy.

Hardware is never the ideal on paper: a real clock drifts, a real sensor

just less code, the physical world needs tuning a minimal model can't see.

Lazy code without its check is unfinished. Non-trivial logic (a branch, a

fixtures, no per-function suites unless asked. Trivial one-liners need no
test, YAGNI applies to tests too.

terse prose). "stop ponytail" / "normal mode": revert. Level persists until
changed or session end.

The shortest path to done is the right path.

## 7. Research gaps and novelty
A gap is reported only when:
1. It is supported by evidence from analysed papers (explicit future-work statements, consistent limitations, contradictions, untested populations/conditions, missing method comparisons).
2. A dedicated novelty check was run: at least 3 targeted searches (`rlab search`) across at least 2 sources, recent years included, plus a web search for very recent work. Queries, date and closest hits are recorded in the gap entry.
3. Confidence is stated. "No paper found" is phrased as "we found no paper that ... (searches on DATE)", never "this has never been studied".

## 8. Copyright and access
----
---
name: find-gaps
description: Identify evidence-backed, novelty-checked research gaps and propose contributions and experiments. Use after methodology comparison, or when the user asks what is missing in the literature or what they could research.
---

# Find research gaps

`rlab` = `python3 scripts/rlab.py`. Rules: [docs/research-standards.md](../../../docs/research-standards.md) §7 (gap and novelty rules) is binding.

Delegate to the `gap-analyst` agent with the project id (it follows these steps); review its report before showing the user.

## 1. Collect candidate gaps
Sources, all in the project: future-work sections (analysis §11), recurring limitations (§8–9), validity threats (§10), contradictions in `evidence-matrix.md`, field-wide weaknesses in `reports/methodology-comparison.md`, RQs with weak or no answer in `RESEARCH-QUESTIONS.md`. Classify each: evidence, methodological, population/context, theoretical, practical, contradiction.

## 2. Evidence test
Keep a candidate only if at least one analysed paper supports it with `[@key, p. N]`; a gap stated by ≥2 independent papers is stronger.

## 3. Novelty check (per surviving candidate)
- ≥3 targeted `rlab search` queries across ≥2 sources, including the last 2 years (`--from`).
- One WebSearch for very recent preprints/work.
- Read titles/abstracts of the closest hits. If a hit fills the gap, drop or narrow the gap. If it is highly relevant, recommend adding it to the project.
Record date, queries and closest hits in the gap entry.

## 4. Contributions and experiments
For each gap: potential contribution, a concrete study design (data, sample, method, baseline, metrics, analysis, expected validity threats), and beginner feasibility (easy/moderate/hard and why).

## 5. Write and check
Fill `gap-report.md` using its template, ranked by evidence strength × feasibility. `rlab cite-check <id> research/<id>/gap-report.md` passes.

Done when: every listed gap has evidence, a recorded novelty check and a confidence rating. Tick Gaps in `STATUS.md`. Tell the user the top 3 gaps in plain language.

1	# Research gap report — LLM-based vs Traditional Static Analysis and Deep Learning Approaches for Source Code Vulnerability Detection: A Comparative Review
2	
3	A gap is only listed when it is backed by evidence from the analysed papers AND a novelty check found no paper already filling it.
4	
5	- Date of all novelty checks: **2026-11-12**. Sources: OpenAlex, arXiv, Crossref (via `rlab search`, raw results in `search/20261112-05*.json`, logged in `search/search-log.md`), plus WebSearch for 2025–2026 work.
6	- Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's data, **[A]** author claim, **[I]** our interpretation. Absence is always phrased as "we found no study that ... (searches on 2026-11-12)".

46	## Positioning of our review
47	
48	**Question.** Does a review or SLR already compare LLM-based, SAST and DL vulnerability detection through an evaluation-setup / benchmark-realism lens, i.e. arguing that benchmark design explains contradictory results?
49	
50	**Verdict.** We found no review that does both of the following (searches on 2026-11-12: Q1–Q5, Q21, Q22, W1, W2):
51	1. synthesises head-to-head evidence across all three families (LLM, SAST, DL) **plus** LLM+SAST hybrids;
52	2. explains specific contradictions between primary studies through their evaluation setup, with a cross-paper comparability audit.
53	
54	Several reviews cover parts of this, so the claim of novelty must be narrow and precise. **Confidence: medium.** Most of the closest new reviews were read at abstract level only, and the field publishes very fast.
55	
56	**The three reviews in our corpus.**
57	
58	| Review | What it covers | How our review differs |
59	|---|---|---|
60	| kaniewski2026systematic (TOSEM SLR, 263 studies to Nov 2025) | LLM-based detection only. Deep analysis of datasets, custom splits and leakage [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 35; @kaniewski2026systematic, p. 38]. Excludes studies that only post-process tool output [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 8]. | It does not cover the LLM-filters-SAST family (C2) and does not synthesise LLM-vs-SAST results. [I] None of its future directions calls for same-benchmark LLM vs SAST vs DL comparisons [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 38]. Its research directions recommend SAST+LLM pipelines [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 42], so our evidence on them complements it. |
61	| zhou2025large (TOSEM SLR, 58 studies to Mar 2024) | LLMs for detection and repair, taxonomy of adaptation techniques. | It predates almost all hybrid, agentic and project-scale evidence. Only one of 40 detection studies was repository-level [@zhou2025large, p. 18]. Its only LLM-vs-SAST study is the authors' own preprint [@zhou2025large, p. 22]. |
62	| sheng2025llms (ACM CSUR narrative survey, 58 studies 2019–2024) | Techniques, datasets and challenges, including leakage and label errors [@sheng2025llms, p. 25]. | It is narrative. It neither compares families on matched results nor ties contradictions to setup. [I] |
63

107	## G1: Published results are not re-scored against trivial baselines or realistic prevalence; no shared evaluation protocol exists for comparing LLMs, SAST and DL
108	- Gap type: methodological
109	- Evidence that the gap exists:
110	  - **Results sit at the flag-everything level.** On 50/50 data, "flag everything" gives F1 0.667. Studies with balanced data report best values at or below that level, and only shu2026evaluating reports the dummy baseline itself:
111	    - shu: the dummy classifier scores 0.6693 against a best of 0.7075 [@shu2026evaluating, p. 11; @shu2026evaluating, p. 17] [V];
112	    - tan: best F1 0.665–0.666 [@tan2026think, p. 7];
113	    - yildiz: GPT F1 48–66 [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 6];
114	    - khare: always-vulnerable rows appear among the best F1 values [@khare2025understanding, p. 16].
115	  - **Class balance flips rankings.**
116	    - shu: fine-tuned GPT-4o wins on balanced data, but PLMs win on the 17%-vulnerable test [@shu2026evaluating, p. 17; @shu2026evaluating, p. 40] [V].
117	    - yildiz: F1 falls from about 49–65 to 5.41–12.21 on non-paired data [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 7] [V].
118	  - **Scoring is unequal between families.**
119	    - gnieciak applies a lenient location rule only to LLMs [@gnieciak2025large, p. 6] [V].
120	    - The CASTLE prompt reveals the scoring scheme to the LLM [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 9] [V].
121	    - Statement-level scoring halves F1 [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 8] [V].
122	  - **Headline LLM-vs-SAST numbers use five incompatible metrics**: macro F1, CASTLE score, accuracy, detection ratio, recall/SFDR [@gnieciak2025large, p. 10; @dubniczky2025castle, p. 10; @khare2025understanding, p. 9; @zhou2024comparison, p. 5; @li2026llm, p. 11] [I].
123	  - **Spurious baselines and random references:**
124	    - a word-count classifier reaches F1 0.86 on BigVul [@risse2025top, p. 11] [V];
125	    - GPT-4 pairwise correctness is below the 22.70% random reference [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9] [V].
126	  - **Statistics are rare.** Only tan2026think applies significance tests to its main comparison [@tan2026think, p. 6] [I, our count].
127	  - **Authors call for guidelines.** yildiz2025benchmarking calls for evaluation guidelines for JIT benchmarking [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 2] [A]. ding2025vulnerability proposes VD-S because accuracy and F1 mislead [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 2] [A].
128	- Novelty check (2026-11-12; Q4, Q5, Q9, Q10 on OpenAlex/arXiv from 2024/2025; W4). Closest hits:
129	  - *Pitfalls in Machine Learning for Computer Security* (CACM 2024, doi:10.1145/3643456) and *Pitfalls in LMs for Code Intelligence* (TOSEM 2025, doi:10.1145/3748647): generic pitfall catalogues with no re-scoring of vulnerability-detection results.
130	  - PrimeVul's VD-S and shu's dummy classifiers are in our corpus; each is applied only within its own study.
131	  - *How much model does warning triage need?* (American Impact Review 2026, doi:10.66308/air.e80134906): re-scores models against a simple reference with MCC and bootstrap CIs, but for actionable-warning triage, not vulnerability detection, and in an unknown-tier venue.
132	  - The CAI 2026 review (doi:10.70267/cai.v3n5.122137) recommends reporting practices but, from its abstract, does not recompute published results.
133	
134	  We found no study that recomputes published LLM, SAST and DL vulnerability-detection results against trivial baselines and realistic prevalence (searches on 2026-11-12).
135	- Confidence: **medium–high**. The evidence comes from ≥6 independent primary studies. The only risk is an unpublished or non-indexed meta-analysis.
136	- Potential contribution: a "re-scored results table" that makes the review's central claim concrete. Many reported LLM advantages may vanish or reverse once compared with flag-all baselines and evaluated at realistic prevalence. It also yields a minimal reporting checklist (confusion matrix, prevalence, trivial baselines, unit and location rule, runs/variance).
137	- Suggested study (secondary analysis of published numbers; no model runs):
138	  - **Data:** results tables of the 16 primary studies (plus any added papers). Extract every (study, tool, dataset, configuration) row that reports enough to rebuild a confusion matrix: TP/FP/FN/TN, or P, R and prevalence.
139	  - **Sample:** all extractable rows. Rows without prevalence or FPR are listed separately, not dropped silently.
140	  - **Method:** for each row compute:
141	    - MCC;
142	    - Youden's J = recall − FPR;
143	    - ΔF1 = F1 − F1_flag-all, where F1_flag-all = 2π/(1+π) and π is prevalence;
144	    - precision at deployment prevalence (π = 1%, 5%, 17%) via P = R·π / (R·π + FPR·(1−π)).
145	  - **Baselines:** always-vulnerable; random (P-C reference 22.70% for ding-style pairs); published dummy or word-count baselines where available.
146	  - **Analysis:** within each study, rank tools before and after re-scoring and count rank reversals (Kendall τ). Do not pool across datasets marked "not comparable" in methodology comparison §3. Report how many rows fail to beat flag-all.
147	  - **Threats:** many rows lack TN/FPR (selection bias); rounding in published tables; lenient TP definitions cannot be undone after the fact; transcription errors (mitigate by double extraction and spot-checking against PDFs).
148	- Feasibility for a beginner: **easy**. Needs only a spreadsheet or about 50 lines of Python, no GPU and no API cost, and takes about 2–4 weeks. It can be included directly in the comparative review as an added-value table.

201	## G3: True-positive loss in LLM filtering of SAST alarms is not controlled per CWE on real security alerts
202	- Gap type: practical / methodological
203	- Evidence that the gap exists:
204	  - **xiong2026sifting.** The best agent configuration cuts OWASP FPR from 98.3% to 6.3% [@xiong2026sifting, p. 12] but drops 22.25% of true vulnerabilities [@xiong2026sifting, p. 18] [V].
205	    - The miss rate is low for injection CWEs (CWE-78 2.38%, CWE-89 1.10%, CWE-79 0.41%) [V].
206	    - It is 77.17% for weak cryptography and 84.50% for weak hashing [@xiong2026sifting, p. 18] [V].
207	    - The authors plan "CWE-aware, cost-adaptive agent strategies and human-in-the-loop" auditing [@xiong2026sifting, p. 20] [A].
208	  - **du2026reducing.** Removes 94–98% of false alarms with real-bug recall of 0.75–0.88 [@du2026reducing, p. 8] [V]. This covers non-security bug types and the authors' own method.
209	  - **Recommended but not evaluated.** kaniewski2026systematic recommends SAST → LLM false-positive filtering pipelines [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 42] [A] but its corpus excludes them [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 8].
210	  - **Real-world samples are small.** xiong uses 50 alerts per set [@xiong2026sifting, p. 13] [V].
211	- Novelty check (2026-11-12; Q13, Q14, Q24 on OpenAlex/arXiv/Crossref from 2024/2025, plus Q25; W5). Closest hits, all not analysed:
212	  - *ZeroFalse* (arXiv 2510.02534): CWE-specific context, high F1 on OWASP/OpenVuln, claims to preserve coverage.
213	  - *Using LLMs to Adjudicate Static-Analysis Alerts with Error Reduction Techniques* (arXiv 2607.09979): consistency checks reach ≥98% recall on Juliet, FormAI and SV-COMP, which are synthetic suites.
214	  - *QASecClaw* (arXiv 2605.01885): multi-agent FP reduction on OWASP.
215	  - *Case-Level Verification in Scanner-LLM Cascades* (arXiv 2610.08406): formalises the FP-reduction vs TPR trade-off, but for DAST.
216	  - *Trusting the Tool* (arXiv 2610.32876): false analyser assurances lower detection of real vulnerabilities by up to 19 points.
217	
218	  These show that TP loss is being measured, and can be reduced on synthetic suites. We found no study that tests a CWE-aware selective filtering policy, i.e. one that filters only CWE classes with demonstrated low miss rates, with held-out evaluation and full FP-reduction vs TP-retention curves on real-world security alerts (searches on 2026-11-12).
219	- Confidence: **low–medium**. This is an active area with many 2025–26 preprints. The gap is narrow and could be filled quickly.
220	- Potential contribution: an operating-point view of alarm filtering, i.e. what share of real vulnerabilities is lost per CWE for a given FP reduction. Also a simple routing policy that practitioners can adopt.
221	- Suggested study:
222	  - **Data:**
223	    - OWASP Benchmark v1.2 (Java, 2,740 labelled cases, official scorer) for development.
224	    - A real-world set of about 100 SAST alerts from post-cutoff open-source Java projects, labelled by two raters (κ), for testing.
225	  - **Method:** run Semgrep and CodeQL; ask 2 open LLMs (7–8B) for a TP/FP verdict with a confidence score, 3 runs.
226	  - **Policies:**
227	    - no filter;
228	    - filter-all (xiong's vanilla);
229	    - CWE-aware filter that applies the LLM only to CWEs whose miss rate was below 5% on a development half of OWASP, evaluated on the other half and on the real set.
230	  - **Metrics:** FP-reduction rate; TP retention; residual FPR; expected triage cost = c_FP·FP + c_FN·FN for cost ratios 1:10 to 1:100.
231	  - **Analysis:** curves across confidence thresholds; per-CWE bootstrap CIs.
232	  - **Threats:** OWASP is synthetic and probably in pre-training data; per-CWE cells are small; rater bias.
233	- Feasibility for a beginner: **easy–moderate**. Ground truth and the scorer are public, Java SAST on OWASP builds easily, and 7B models run locally. Expect 4–6 weeks. The main effort is labelling the real-world alerts.

235	## G4: Hybrid LLM+SAST detectors lack independent replication that separates target, metric and labeller effects
236	- Gap type: contradiction / evidence
237	- Evidence that the gap exists:
238	  - **RepoAudit: author evaluation vs independent evaluation.**
239	    - Authors: 78.43% precision and all 21 known bugs reproduced, one run per setting [@guo2025repoaudit, p. 8; @guo2025repoaudit, p. 17] [V].
240	    - Independent (li2026llm): 0 of 110 known C/C++ vulnerabilities and 92.77% SFDR [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 11] [V]; cost up to $1,247.66 per project [@li2026llm, p. 16] [V].
241	  - **IRIS: author evaluation vs independent evaluation.**
242	    - Authors: 55 vs 27 of 120 CVEs detected compared with CodeQL [@li2024iris, p. 8] [V].
243	    - Independent: 97.80% vs 77.00% SFDR on new Java projects [@li2026llm, p. 12] [V].
244	  - **The independent study labels with an LLM it also evaluates.** li2026llm labels warnings with Codex, which it also evaluates [@li2026llm, p. 11] [V], so its labeller is not independent [I].
245	  - **The gain depends on a strong LLM.** IRIS gains depend on GPT-4; smaller LLMs worsen FDR [@li2024iris, p. 10] [V].
246	  - **Neither paper settles the discrepancy** (methodology comparison §4, C2/C6) [I].
247	- Novelty check (2026-11-12; Q11, Q12, Q23 on arXiv/OpenAlex/Crossref from 2024/2025; W3). Closest hits:
248	  - li2026llm (in corpus) is itself the only independent re-evaluation.
249	  - *What Survives the Next Model?* (arXiv 2609.00468): re-runs ICSE 2026 technique papers against single prompts, across SE tasks generally.
250	  - *Trusting the Tool* (arXiv 2610.32876): studies LLM deference to analyser evidence, not tool replication.
251	  - Agent tools found (Revelio arXiv 2606.22263, AnyPoC arXiv 2604.11950) are new tools, not replications.
252	
253	  We found no study that re-runs IRIS or RepoAudit on the authors' original benchmark and on new targets, under the same blinded human labelling, so that the discrepancy can be attributed (searches on 2026-11-12).
254	- Confidence: **medium**. Reproductions may exist in artifact-evaluation reports that are not indexed.
255	- Potential contribution: tells practitioners whether published hybrid gains transfer to new code. It also tells researchers which evaluation choices (targets, metric, labeller, model version) drive the reported differences.
256	- Suggested study:
257	  - **Design:** 2 × 2 factorial — target set (original CWE-Bench-Java subset vs post-cutoff Java CVEs) × metric (the original "detected CVE" metric vs sampled false-discovery rate), on the **same** runs.
258	  - **Data:** 30 CWE-Bench-Java CVEs across 4 CWEs, plus 10–15 post-cutoff Java CVEs. IRIS code and data are public [@li2024iris, p. 2].
259	  - **Arms:** IRIS with the original LLM family where affordable, and with one open model; CodeQL alone as baseline.
260	  - **Labelling:** a random sample of ≥100 warnings labelled by two humans blinded to the tool (κ reported).
261	  - **Metrics:** detections, FDR/SFDR, cost (tokens, USD, time).
262	  - **Threats:** model deprecation (GPT-4 versions); CodeQL version drift; build failures; API cost.
263	- Feasibility for a beginner: **moderate–hard**. Building Java projects for CodeQL and running a hybrid pipeline is demanding. A reduced IRIS-only replication on 20–30 CVEs with an open model is feasible in about 8 weeks. RepoAudit (C/C++, high token cost) is not recommended for a beginner.

285	    - *Exploring Automated Vulnerability Identification in JavaScript Code Using LLMs* (arXiv 2609.13816): snippet-level, LLM vs SAST.
286	  - PHP: *WordPress plugin benchmark* (doi:10.3390/bdcc10090303): a static taint analyser vs ML/DL, no LLM. The taint analyser misses about 98% of vulnerabilities (abstract only).
287	  - *Vulnerability Detection with Interprocedural Context in Multiple Languages* (arXiv 2604.08417): LLMs only, C/C++/Python.
288	  - *A Preliminary Study of LLMs for Multilingual Vulnerability Detection* (ISSTA companion 2025, doi:10.1145/3713081.3731746): PLMs vs LLMs, no SAST.
289	
290	  We found no study comparing LLMs with SAST on real CVEs at repository level for PHP or Go, and only snippet-level or synthetic-repository evidence for JavaScript and Python (searches on 2026-11-12).
291	- Confidence: **low–medium**. Python and JavaScript are being filled quickly. The gap is clearest for PHP and Go.
292	- Potential contribution: tests whether the "LLM higher recall, lower precision" pattern holds in web languages, where injection CWEs (which LLMs handle best [@xiong2026sifting, p. 18]) dominate.
293	- Suggested study:
294	  - **Data:** about 60 real PHP CVEs (e.g. from the released WordPress-plugin benchmark data) or Go CVEs from the Go vulnerability database (OSV).
295	  - **Arms:** Semgrep (supports both languages), a language-specific SAST tool, and 2 open LLMs at file level with retrieved callers. Check CodeQL's supported-language list for the chosen language before planning a CodeQL arm.
296	  - **Metrics:** recall on known CVEs; precision on a manually labelled warning sample; cost.
297	  - **Analysis:** per-CWE recall with CIs.
298	  - **Threats:** label quality (the WordPress paper finds 48.8% of cleaned positives genuine, abstract only); small samples; tool coverage differences.
299	- Feasibility for a beginner: **moderate**. The tools are free and build-free for PHP and Go. The main cost is manual labelling of warnings.
300	
301	## G6: No cost-per-confirmed-vulnerability comparison across LLM, SAST and DL including human triage effort
302	- Gap type: practical
303	- Evidence that the gap exists:
304	  - **Most studies report no monetary cost.** Ten of 16 primary studies report none [I, our count]. The six that do are du, guo, li2026llm, shu, tan and xiong [@du2026reducing, p. 8; @guo2025repoaudit, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 16; @shu2026evaluating, p. 42; @tan2026think, p. 10; @xiong2026sifting, p. 17].
305	  - **Where measured, cost is decisive.**
306	    - Per project: from $2.54 in the RepoAudit paper to $172.77 on average and $1,247.66 at most in li2026llm [@guo2025repoaudit, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 16] [V].
307	    - Thinking mode costs 2.7–4.4× the energy [@tan2026think, p. 10] [V].
308	  - **Cost is not linked to triage effort.** None of the cost figures is expressed per confirmed true positive, including the analyst time spent on false warnings [I]. li2026llm calls for cost-aware designs [@li2026llm, p. 18] [A].
309	- Novelty check (2026-11-12; Q15, Q16, Q25 on OpenAlex/arXiv/Crossref from 2024/2025; W7). Closest hits:
310	  - *Open or Frontier?* (Computers 2026, doi:10.3390/computers15090623): measures cost and energy for 8 LLMs vs a fine-tuned detector, with precision at 1:44 prevalence. **No SAST, no triage effort.** This narrows the gap considerably.
311	  - *Vulnerability Detection with Interprocedural Context in Multiple Languages* (arXiv 2604.08417): cost per LLM configuration only.
312	  - Vendor blogs (Semgrep, Endor Labs) report cost per true positive for their own products; these are not peer-reviewed and have conflicts of interest.
313	
314	  We found no peer-reviewed study reporting cost per confirmed vulnerability, including triage time, for all three families on the same targets (searches on 2026-11-12).
315	- Confidence: **low–medium**. The gap is narrowed by *Open or Frontier?*. What remains is the SAST arm and the triage-effort term.
316	- Potential contribution: a decision-oriented metric for practitioners: dollars and analyst minutes per real vulnerability found.
317	- Suggested study: measure as a secondary outcome of G2 (same targets). Record compute cost per arm, then time two raters triaging a random 50 warnings per arm. Cost per TP = (compute + triage minutes × hourly rate) / confirmed TPs, reported with sensitivity bands for hourly rates. Threats: triage time depends on rater skill; API price changes.
318	- Feasibility for a beginner: **moderate**. It is cheap if added to G2, but on its own it needs the same infrastructure.

# Open or Frontier? A Cost- and Energy-Aware Benchmark of Large Language Models for Software Vulnerability Detection

- Authors: Deininger, Patrick; Slany, Wolfgang
- Year / venue: 2026, Computers (published)
- DOI: 10.3390/computers15090623 · URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/computers15090623
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)

Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.

## 1. Research objective
[A] To benchmark open-weight against frontier LLMs on function-level vulnerability detection, treating monetary cost and energy as "first-class axes alongside detection quality" (p. 1). The study also calibrates the LLM results against non-LLM reference points (static analysers and learned detectors) "to gauge absolute difficulty" (p. 2). [A] The authors claim the conjunction is new (a security task, a five-model open roster, and cost and energy as per-task axes), "not ... a priority" on any single axis (p. 3).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- [V] No numbered RQs. Contributions are framed as (p. 2):
  - a cost- and energy-aware open-vs-frontier benchmark on label-clean PrimeVul with non-LLM reference points;
  - evidence on the quality–efficiency Pareto frontier;
  - an account of what can and cannot be measured for closed API models.
- [I] Implicit questions:
  1. Are open-weight LLMs competitive with frontier LLMs in quality?
  2. Are they more cost- and energy-efficient?
  3. How do LLMs compare with SAST and fine-tuned detectors at realistic prevalence?

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: [V] Empirical benchmark of binary function-level detection ("does this C/C++ function contain a vulnerability?") on a fixed stratified PrimeVul sample (p. 4). Additional analyses (pp. 9–20):
  - re-scoring at the natural 1:44 prevalence;
  - configuration-matched families A/B/C;
  - prompt, sample-draw and run-to-run robustness;
  - a reasoning-vs-direct replication across two measurement epochs.
- Approach / model / intervention: [V] Eight LLMs prompted zero-shot through a unified OpenAI-compatible API gateway (p. 4, Table 2). [V] The gateway is **not named** (pp. 4, 29).
  - **Frontier:** Claude Sonnet 5, GPT-5.1, Gemini 3.1 Pro (`gemini-3.1-pro-preview`); active parameters assumed ~100B for the energy estimate.
  - **Open-weight:** DeepSeek-V3.2 (~37B active), GLM-5 (~32B active), Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen3-Coder-30B (3B active MoE), Gemma-3-4B.
  - [V] Pinned providers and precision: DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5 at GMICloud FP8; Llama-3.3-70B at DeepInfra FP8; Qwen3-Coder-30B at SiliconFlow FP8; Gemma-3-4B at DeepInfra bf16 (p. 29, Table A2).
  - [V] Main configuration: direct answer, reasoning disabled where permitted. Gemini cannot disable reasoning (HTTP 400) (p. 4, p. 29).
  - [V] Prompt: a security-reviewer persona; answer YES/NO first, then an optional explanation (p. 28). A lenient parser counts unparseable outputs as parse failures, not "safe" (p. 4, p. 29).
- Baselines or comparison conditions:
  - [V] **Trivial baselines:** always-safe and always-vulnerable (p. 7, Table 4); always-flag at 1:44 prevalence (p. 8, Table 5).
  - [V] **SAST arm** (p. 6, p. 10, Table 7): Flawfinder 2.0.20 (lexical), Cppcheck 2.21 (flow-sensitive), Semgrep 1.175 with community C and security-audit rulesets (pattern plus intraprocedural taint). A function is flagged if any finding reaches a swept severity threshold.
  - [V] **DL arm:**
    - CodeBERT fine-tuned on Devign (off the shelf, cross-dataset, argmax, 512 tokens) (p. 6);
    - CodeBERT (125M) fine-tuned on PrimeVul's training split, with the threshold selected on the validation split (p. 10–11).
  - [V] **CodeQL was not run.** PrimeVul functions are isolated snippets with no build, so no CodeQL database can be built (p. 10–11).

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): [V] PrimeVul test split (C/C++): 24,788 functions after loading, 549 vulnerable — "a realistic 1:44 class ratio" (p. 4).
- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] N = 1549 functions: all 549 vulnerable plus 1000 seeded-random safe functions (p. 4). [I] Prevalence in the evaluated sample is 35.4% (549/1549). This is **not** 50/50, although the text once calls it "balanced by construction" (p. 8). [V] The effective N per model is 1526–1549 because parse failures are excluded (p. 6).
- Sampling / selection method:
  - [V] Label-stratified sample fixed by seed (p. 4).
  - [V] Two further near-disjoint safe pools (<6% overlap) were drawn for robustness (p. 19).
  - [V] LLM inputs were truncated to 8000 characters. This affects 105/1549 functions and 87/549 (15.8%) of the vulnerable ones; non-LLM baselines see untruncated code (p. 4).
  - [V] All CVEs date from 2008–2022 and predate the models' training cutoffs (p. 24). [V] The PrimeVul training split contains no evaluated function or function body (up to whitespace) (p. 10, p. 25).
- Data availability (public? link?): [V] Released on Zenodo (doi 10.5281/zenodo.21391073): harness, configurations, sampled function IDs, price snapshot, energy sweep, baseline scores and aggregated results (p. 26). [V] PrimeVul is fetched from its original authors by script; the fine-tuned checkpoint is regenerable by script (p. 26).

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools:
  - [V] Harness and decoding: a test-driven harness with 82 automated tests; temperature 0, seed 12345, one generation per item; output budget 64 tokens in the matched configuration (256 for two frontier models in the first epoch) (p. 6, p. 29).
  - [V] Cost: computed from logged input/output tokens × list price at a pinned provider, with gateway fallbacks disabled (p. 5).
  - [V] Provider price dispersion: up to 14.4× for DeepSeek-V3.2 (USD 0.209–3.000 per million input tokens) (p. 5, Table 3).
  - [V] Energy (p. 5):
    - FLOP estimate E ≈ 2·N_active·T·ε for API-served models;
    - measured with the NVML energy counter on a dedicated NVIDIA H200 for locally servable open models (concurrency 1, idle-subtracted "active" energy);
    - plus a concurrency sweep c = 1/8/32/64 (p. 14, Table 9).
  - [V] Latency: client-side under concurrency 10, so it conflates queueing (p. 30).
  - [V] Statistics: stratified paired bootstrap of balanced-accuracy differences (20,000 resamples, seed 12,345) with Holm correction over a 9-comparison primary family and a 15-comparison strict family (p. 6, p. 28).
- Code availability: [V] The harness and configurations are released (p. 6, p. 26).

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
  - [V] **Balanced accuracy** is the primary metric, because accuracy is dominated by the always-safe classifier (0.646 accuracy, above every LLM) and both trivial classifiers score exactly 0.5 on it (p. 6).
  - [V] MCC and F1 are also reported (p. 6).
  - [V] Deployment metrics at 1:44 prevalence are derived from the prevalence-invariant TPR/FPR (p. 8, Table 5):
    - precision; false positives per true positive (FP/TP);
    - alerts and found vulnerabilities per 1000 functions;
    - **USD per true positive** and **kJ per true positive**.
  - [V] Elicited 0–100 confidence gives ROC-AUC where usable. VD-Score is declined because the coarse score grids cannot reach its 0.5% FPR point (p. 9–10).
- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals):
  - [V] Paired bootstrap 95% CIs and Holm-adjusted p for open-vs-frontier gaps (p. 27, Table A1).
  - [V] Wilson-based 95% CIs on precision at deployment prevalence for the non-LLM baselines (p. 10, Table 7).
  - [V] Robustness: Spearman rank correlation across prompts and draws (p. 19, Table 13).
  - [V] Output-budget effects are tested with a paired bootstrap (p. 16, Table 10).

## 7. Key findings
1. **Detection quality, first epoch** — [V] Balanced accuracy / F1 per model, direct mode, N = 1549 (p. 7, Table 4). [V] F1 range across LLMs is 0.405–0.615 vs always-vulnerable F1 0.523 (p. 7, Table 4).

   | Model | Bal. acc. (95% CI) | F1 |
   |---|---|---|
   | DeepSeek-V3.2 | 0.676 (0.654–0.697) | 0.615 |
   | Gemma-3-4B | 0.653 | 0.590 |
   | GLM-5 | 0.637 | 0.596 |
   | Gemini-3.1-Pro | 0.623 | 0.591 |
   | GPT-5.1 | 0.617 | 0.560 |
   | Claude-Sonnet-5 | 0.616 | 0.582 |
   | Llama-3.3-70B | 0.604 | 0.578 |
   | Qwen3-Coder-30B | 0.511 | 0.405 |

2. **Open vs frontier significance** — [V] DeepSeek-V3.2 significantly beats all three frontier models: +0.054 to +0.060 balanced accuracy, Holm p < 5×10⁻⁴ (p. 6, p. 27, Table A1).
   - [V] Gemma-3-4B beats Claude-Sonnet-5 (+0.037, Holm p = 0.032); the other top-open gaps are not significant (p. 7, p. 27).
   - [V] Qwen3-Coder-30B is indistinguishable from chance (MCC 0.022, CI −0.03 to 0.07) (p. 7).
3. **Budget-matched second epoch (Family A)** — [V] Balanced accuracy / MCC: DeepSeek-V3.2 0.711 / 0.403; GLM-5 0.669 / 0.352; Gemma-3-4B 0.653 / 0.297; Claude-Sonnet-5 0.653 / 0.321; GPT-5.1 0.615 / 0.225; Llama 0.609 / 0.267; Qwen 0.568 / 0.136; Gemini 0.606 / 0.252, on only the 54.2% of tasks it answered (p. 17, Table 11).
   - [V] Claude equals Gemma (+0.0003, p = 0.98) (p. 17).
   - [V] Absolute numbers shifted by up to 0.06 between epochs seven weeks apart ("service drift") (p. 7–8, p. 20).
4. **Reasoning mode** — [V] Reasoning helps every frontier model (Claude +0.032, GPT-5.1 +0.044, Gemini +0.096) but hurts DeepSeek-V3.2 (−0.133, p < 10⁻⁴) and does not help GLM-5 (−0.019, n.s.); it costs 4.5–12.1× more per task (p. 17–18, Table 12).
   - [V] Best observed: DeepSeek 0.711 (direct) vs Claude 0.685 and Gemini 0.680 (reasoning); DeepSeek vs Claude p = 0.081 (p. 17).
   - [V] Reasoning lowers DeepSeek's specificity from 0.52 to 0.37 (p. 20).
5. **Prompt sensitivity dominates** — [V] Two paraphrases move balanced accuracy by up to 0.088 and produce three different winners (DeepSeek 0.711, Claude 0.741, GLM-5 0.700); Spearman ρ vs anchor = 0.381 and 0.810 (p. 19–20, Table 13).
   - [V] Safe-pool redraws move scores ≤0.015 (ρ = 1.000) (p. 19).
   - [V] Temperature-0 verdict agreement is 88.3–100%; only Gemma is exactly reproducible (p. 19).
6. **SAST baselines on the same functions** (p. 7, p. 10, Table 4, Table 7) — balanced accuracy / recall / specificity / precision at 1:44:
   - [V] Flawfinder risk≥1: 0.589 / 0.271 / 0.907 / 6.20%; risk≥4: 0.523 / 0.055 / 0.992 / 13.40%.
   - [V] Cppcheck: 0.548–0.592 balanced accuracy; precision 2.46–3.77%.
   - [V] Semgrep severity≥INFO: 0.514 / 0.031 / 0.998 / 25.96% (CI 5.7–66.9%). It flags 19 of 1549 functions with 17 TP and 2 FP (p. 11).
   - [V] Flawfinder is "ahead of every LLM at every threshold" on deployment precision but finds almost nothing (p. 9, p. 23).
7. **Fine-tuned DL baseline beats every LLM** — [V] CodeBERT-PrimeVul (125M, validation-tuned threshold) reaches balanced accuracy 0.765, MCC 0.526, recall 0.709, specificity 0.821, precision 8.23% at 1:44 (CI 6.9–9.7) and ROC-AUC 0.845 (p. 10, Table 7; p. 10–11). [V] CodeBERT-Devign (cross-dataset) collapses to 0.518, flagging 97% of functions (p. 7, p. 23). [V] At argmax 0.5 the PrimeVul detector predicts all-safe because no score exceeds 0.372. The authors "nearly reported" this artefact as evidence that trained detectors are no better than LLMs (p. 11).
8. **Deployment at 1:44 prevalence** — [V] Every LLM's precision is 2.3–3.8% vs 2.21% for always-flag; FP/TP ranges from 25.6 (DeepSeek) to 41.9 (Qwen); models alert on 43–75% of functions (p. 8, Table 5). [A] "Neither is ready for independent use" (p. 9).
9. **Cost per task** — [V] USD/task, first epoch (p. 7, Table 4); SAST and CodeBERT-Devign cost ≈0:

   | Model | USD/task |
   |---|---|
   | DeepSeek-V3.2 | 0.00017 |
   | Gemma-3-4B | 0.00004 |
   | GLM-5 | 0.00048 |
   | Gemini-3.1-Pro | 0.00448 |
   | GPT-5.1 | 0.00139 |
   | Claude-Sonnet-5 | 0.00441 |
   | Llama-3.3-70B | 0.00008 |
   | Qwen3-Coder-30B | 0.00006 |

   - [V] Family A cost (p. 17, Table 11): DeepSeek 0.00015, Claude 0.00265, Gemini 0.00219 USD/task.
   - [V] Gemma matches Claude's Family A quality at 1/66 of the cost; DeepSeek beats Claude at 1/18 (p. 17).
10. **Energy per task** — [V] J/task (p. 7, Table 4); frontier values are FLOP estimates at an assumed 100B active parameters, with the 25–400B sweep in brackets:

    | Model | J/task | Source |
    |---|---|---|
    | DeepSeek-V3.2 | 526 | estimated |
    | Gemma-3-4B | 64 | estimated |
    | GLM-5 | 424 | estimated |
    | Gemini-3.1-Pro | 1966 [492–7865] | estimated |
    | GPT-5.1 | 1332 [333–5329] | estimated |
    | Claude-Sonnet-5 | 2489 [622–9955] | estimated |
    | Llama-3.3-70B | 738 | measured |
    | Qwen3-Coder-30B | 88 | measured |

    - [V] Concurrency sweep on an H200 (c = 1 → 64), J/task: Gemma 84.4 → 3.8; Qwen 84.0 → 7.5; Llama 739.9 → 74.2. The FLOP estimator overstates batched energy by 5.4–16.9× (p. 14, Table 9).
    - [A] API-served energies are "most likely" overstated by about an order of magnitude (p. 14).
11. **Cost and energy per detected vulnerability (G6)** — [V] At 1:44 prevalence (p. 8, Table 5):

    | Model | USD per TP | kJ per TP |
    |---|---|---|
    | Gemma-3-4B | 0.003 | 3.7 |
    | Llama-3.3-70B | 0.004 | 44.8 |
    | Qwen3-Coder-30B | 0.006 | 4.0 |
    | DeepSeek-V3.2 | 0.009 | 28.4 |
    | GLM-5 | 0.023 | 20.3 |
    | GPT-5.1 | 0.082 | 78.3 |
    | Gemini-3.1-Pro | 0.210 | 92.4 |
    | Claude-Sonnet-5 | 0.212 | 119.6 |

    - [V] Flawfinder: ≈0 cost per TP (p. 8, Table 5).
    - [V] USD/TP is not reported for CodeBERT-PrimeVul ("negligible inference cost", p. 11) or for Cppcheck/Semgrep (pp. 8–11).
    - [V] **Human triage effort is not included**: these are compute costs per TP surfaced, with 25.6–41.9 false positives per TP (p. 8).
12. **Self-hosting economics** — [V] At concurrency 64 on one H200, self-hosting is cheaper than the API for Gemma and Qwen (0.15–0.36× API price) (p. 22, Table 14). For Llama-3.3-70B it is 0.63× on owned hardware but 1.50× on a rented card. These are GPU-time-only assumptions (USD 3.50/h rented; USD 1.46/h owned).
13. **Contamination gradient** — [V] Recall on pre-2020 CVEs is 7–15 points higher than on 2021–2022 CVEs for better-balanced models (e.g. GPT-5.1 0.88 vs 0.73; DeepSeek 0.90 vs 0.81) (p. 24). [A] This is "consistent with some memorization" (p. 24).
14. **Elicited confidence** — [V] Only Claude used the requested probability scale (ROC-AUC 0.814); three models reported verdict confidence instead (converted AUC 0.69–0.76); DeepSeek emitted −1 on 1409/1549 tasks; Gemini produced a parseable pair on 1.2% of tasks (p. 9, Table 6).
15. **Trivial-baseline comparison** — [I] Our reading of Table 4 (p. 7):
    - Sample (35.4% positive): best LLM F1 0.615 is only +0.092 above always-vulnerable F1 0.523; Qwen (0.405) is below it. The 0.667 balanced-data reference does not apply at this prevalence.
    - At 1:44 prevalence, our calculation from Table 5 TPR and precision (p. 8): always-flag F1 ≈ 0.043; best LLM (DeepSeek) F1 ≈ 0.072; CodeBERT-PrimeVul ≈ 0.147; Flawfinder risk≥1 ≈ 0.101. Flawfinder's F1 is above every LLM's at deployment prevalence.

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] Energy is measured for only some open models; frontier energy rests on an untested active-parameter assumption and is reported as a sensitivity range (p. 23).
- [A] Configuration asymmetries: Gemini cannot run without reasoning; two frontier models needed larger output budgets in the main run (p. 24).
- [A] Latency is confounded by queueing (p. 24).
- [A] Training-data contamination: all CVEs are 2008–2022 and may appear in pre-training; absolute scores "may be optimistic"; a post-cutoff restriction is planned (p. 24).
- [A] One prompt, one draw and one generation in the headline table; variation across datasets and task formulations remains unbounded (p. 24).
- [A] Serving-layer dependence (p. 24–25):
  - price spread up to 14×;
  - two silent serving faults: billed empty outputs, and a reasoning flag ignored with HTTP 200;
  - quality is robust to provider and precision for Llama (0.599–0.609).
- [A] CodeQL cannot be applied to unbuildable function snippets (p. 25).
- [A] Scope: one dataset, one task formulation, function level only; other languages and statement-level localisation are future work (p. 25).
- [A] "No result here should be read as evidence that function-level vulnerability triage is ready for independent use" (p. 26).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] **Internal inconsistencies from revision** (the paper went through at least one major review round, p. 1, pp. 16–19):
  - Gemma-3-4B is said to be incompatible with the local vLLM/CUDA build, so its energy is FLOP-estimated (p. 6, p. 15). Yet Table 9 reports a measured concurrency sweep for Gemma (p. 14), and the abstract says three open models were measured (p. 1), while p. 5 says two.
  - The limitations list says a fine-tuned PrimeVul detector "is the remaining gap" (p. 25), but Section 4.4 reports exactly such a detector (p. 10–11).
  - The reasoning cost multiplier is "2.5 to 7.6 times" on p. 24 vs 4.5–12.1× in Table 12 (p. 18); these are different epochs, but the text does not say so.
  - The sample is called "balanced by construction" (p. 8) although it is 35.4% positive (p. 4).
  - These are reporting slips, not evidence of wrong numbers, but readers should cite table values rather than prose.
- [I] **The SAST arm is weak by design for C/C++.** Flawfinder, Cppcheck and Semgrep community rules on isolated functions, with no CodeQL, Infer or commercial tools (p. 10–11). The comparison is LLM vs lightweight function-level SAST, not vs semantic whole-program SAST.
- [I] **Not post-cutoff** (CVEs 2008–2022, p. 24), and the measured recall gradient by CVE year suggests memorisation. The LLM-vs-fine-tuned comparison is also asymmetric: the fine-tuned model is in-distribution, while the LLMs are zero-shot (p. 11).
- [I] **Cost per TP excludes triage.** With 25.6–41.9 FP per TP (p. 8), analyst time would dominate compute cost (cents per TP). The paper's USD/TP therefore understates the practical cost per confirmed vulnerability by a large factor.
- [I] **Unnamed gateway** and preview model identifiers (`gemini-3.1-pro-preview`, p. 29) limit long-term reproducibility. The service drift of up to 0.06 between epochs (p. 20) shows API results are time-stamped observations.
- [I] **Function-level, C/C++ only** — no repository context. The truncation at 8000 characters affects 15.8% of positives (p. 4).
- [I] **AI-assisted writing and code.** The authors used Claude Opus 5/Sonnet 5 to draft text and write Python code (p. 27), and Claude-Sonnet-5 is one of the evaluated models. This is disclosed and the data are stated to be the authors' own; we note it for transparency, not as a conflict.

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection):
  - [V] Train/test separation for CodeBERT-PrimeVul is verified: no evaluated function or body is in training (p. 25).
  - [V] Thresholds are tuned on validation, not test (sweeping on test would give 0.777 vs the reported 0.765) (p. 11).
  - [V] Contamination is not controlled but is measured as a recall gradient by CVE year (p. 24).
  - [V] Epoch drift is handled by within-epoch comparisons (p. 16–18).
  - [V] Parse failures are excluded, not recoded (p. 27).
- External (generalisability of sample/context):
  - [V] One dataset (PrimeVul), C/C++, function level (p. 25).
  - [I] It is unclear whether results hold for repository-level detection or other languages.
  - [I] Model versions are a 2026 snapshot.
- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?):
  - [V] Balanced accuracy is chosen deliberately; the paper shows its ranking differs from the precision ranking at deployment prevalence (GPT-5.1 3rd on precision, 5th on balanced accuracy) (p. 8–9).
  - [I] PrimeVul labels are "near-human-accuracy" per its authors (p. 3), but no own label audit was done.
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance):
  - [V] Paired bootstrap with Holm correction; families are declared explicitly (p. 28).
  - [V] Prompt variance (≤0.088) exceeds most between-model gaps (p. 19–20). [A] "No single-prompt ranking of LLMs on this task should be read as a property of the models" (p. 20).
  - [V] Deployment precision CIs are reported for the non-LLM rows and the best/weakest LLM (p. 10, Table 7).
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?):
  - [V] Strong: harness, configurations, prompts, parser rules, pinned providers and prices, function IDs and energy data are released (p. 26, pp. 28–30).
  - [V] API non-determinism remains: 0–12% of verdicts flip at temperature 0 (p. 19).

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A]:
  - calibrate the FLOP energy estimator against measured batched energy, per architecture (p. 26);
  - corroborate on a second dataset and task formulation (p. 26);
  - post-cutoff CVEs or paired PrimeVul variants to bound memorisation (p. 24);
  - controlled single-request latency (p. 24);
  - other languages, statement-level localisation, and VD-Score at realistic imbalance (p. 25).
- Suggested by us [I]:
  - Add triage time per alert to turn USD/TP into cost per confirmed vulnerability (G6).
  - Run a semantic SAST arm at repository level, where builds exist.
  - Repeat with post-cutoff functions so that the fine-tuned vs zero-shot comparison is contamination-free (G2).

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1 (primary: LLM vs SAST vs fine-tuned DL on identical functions), RQ2, RQ3 (cost/energy trade-offs; no hybrid), RQ5.
- How it informs our work [I]:
  - **RQ1:** one of very few same-benchmark three-family comparisons. The ranking depends on the metric:
    - on balanced accuracy: fine-tuned CodeBERT > best LLMs > Flawfinder/Cppcheck > Semgrep;
    - on precision at realistic prevalence: Semgrep (26.0%) and strict-threshold Flawfinder (13.4%) > CodeBERT (8.2%) > lenient Flawfinder (6.2%) > all LLMs (2.3–3.8%). Cppcheck (2.5–3.8%) sits in the LLM range (p. 10, Table 7);
    - all are far from deployable.
  - This fits our "LLMs higher recall, lower precision" pattern and C3/C5.
  - **Correction for our gap report.** The G2 and G6 novelty-check notes describe *Open or Frontier?* as "No SAST". That is **incorrect**: Flawfinder 2.0.20, Cppcheck 2.21 and Semgrep 1.175 are run on the identical 1549 functions (p. 6, p. 10). G2 is therefore narrowed further: a same-benchmark LLM + SAST + fine-tuned DL comparison now exists at function level on C/C++. What is still missing is post-cutoff code, repository level, and semantic SAST.
  - **G6 is narrowed further.** USD/TP and kJ/TP at 1:44 prevalence are reported for 8 LLMs (p. 8). The remaining gap is the triage-effort term and a costed SAST/DL arm (≈0 is not quantified per TP).
  - **G1:** a further study that reports trivial baselines and realistic-prevalence re-scoring. It shows LLM precision barely above always-flag (2.3–3.8% vs 2.21%).
  - **C1:** the argmax-collapse artefact (p. 11) suggests some reports of fine-tuned models being near chance on PrimeVul may reflect decision thresholds rather than ranking ability. This is a candidate explanation, not established for other papers.
  - **C4:** reasoning raises frontier balanced accuracy but lowers DeepSeek's specificity (more false positives) (p. 17, p. 20). This supports the "model-dependent" reading.

## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RQ1 | On 1549 PrimeVul C/C++ functions (35.4% vulnerable), zero-shot LLM balanced accuracy 0.511–0.676 (first epoch) and 0.568–0.711 (budget-matched epoch); best DeepSeek-V3.2 | 7, 17 | V | moderate (single dataset, prompt-sensitive) |
| RQ1 | Fine-tuned CodeBERT-PrimeVul (125M, validation-tuned threshold) beats every LLM: bal. acc. 0.765, MCC 0.526, precision at 1:44 8.23% vs best LLM 0.711 / 0.403 / ≤4.62% | 10, 11, 17 | V | moderate (in-distribution vs zero-shot) |
| RQ1 | Same functions, SAST: Flawfinder bal. acc. 0.589 (risk≥1), Cppcheck 0.548–0.592, Semgrep 0.501–0.514 (recall 0.002–0.031); SAST more precise at 1:44 (Flawfinder 6.2–13.4%, Semgrep 26.0% [5.7–66.9]) than every LLM (2.3–3.8%) | 7, 9, 10, 11 | V | moderate (lightweight SAST only; no CodeQL) |
| RQ1 | Trivial baselines: always-vulnerable F1 0.523 vs LLM F1 0.405–0.615; at 1:44 every LLM's precision 2.3–3.8% vs always-flag 2.21%, 25.6–41.9 FP per TP | 7, 8 | V | moderate |
| RQ2 | Prompt paraphrase moves bal. acc. up to 0.088 and changes the winner (ρ vs anchor 0.381); safe-pool redraw ≤0.015; temperature-0 verdict agreement 88.3–100% | 19, 20 | V | moderate |
| RQ2 | Recall on pre-2020 CVEs 7–15 points higher than 2021–2022 for better-balanced LLMs (memorisation signal) | 24 | V | weak–moderate (no significance test reported) |
| RQ2 | Argmax decision rule made the fine-tuned detector look like always-safe (bal. acc. 0.500) despite ROC-AUC 0.845; threshold choice can flip LLM-vs-DL conclusions | 11 | V | moderate |
| RQ3 | Cost per task: open USD 0.00004–0.00048 vs frontier 0.00139–0.00448; Gemma-3-4B matches Claude-Sonnet-5 quality at 1/66 cost; reasoning costs 4.5–12.1× more | 7, 17, 18 | V | moderate (list prices, provider-dependent up to 14×) |
| RQ3 | Cost and energy per true positive at 1:44: USD 0.003 (Gemma) to 0.212 (Claude); 3.7 to 119.6 kJ; excludes human triage of 25.6–41.9 FP per TP | 8 | V | moderate (compute only) |
| RQ3 | Energy per task: measured 88 J (Qwen3-Coder-30B) and 738 J (Llama-3.3-70B); frontier FLOP-estimated 1332–2489 J (range 333–9955); batching cuts measured energy 10–22× | 7, 14 | V | weak–moderate (frontier estimated) |
| RQ5 | Authors: no method tested (LLM, SAST, fine-tuned DL) is ready for independent function-level triage | 26 | A | moderate |

## 14. Key quotes
> "at the natural 1:44 prevalence, precision is 2.3–8.2%" (p. 1)

> "The LLMs flag nearly everything and are almost never right; the static analyzer flags almost nothing and is right somewhat more often." (p. 9)

> "Three reasonable phrasings of the same question produce three different winners." (p. 20)

> "No single-prompt ranking of LLMs on this task should be read as a property of the models; it is a property of the pair (model, prompt)." (p. 20)

## Analyst notes
- Reading coverage: All 32 pages read from `fulltext.txt`, including appendices A–B and references. Figures 1–3 (pp. 12–13) are plots whose values are also given in Tables 4 and 9 and in the text; they were not re-read from the PDF.
- Uncertainties:
  - Revision inconsistencies about which models had energy measured (see §9). Table values were used where prose and tables disagree.
  - Which figures are "first epoch" and which are "second epoch" matters. Table 4/5 cost and energy are first epoch (p. 8); Family A quality (Table 11) is second epoch.
  - The F1 values at 1:44 prevalence are our calculation from reported TPR and precision, not reported by the paper.
  - The gap-report G2/G6 entries need correcting: this paper does include SAST baselines.
