# A Real CVE-Backed Benchmark for WordPress Plugin Vulnerability Detection: Re-Evaluating Static and Learning-Based Detectors Under Leakage-Controlled Evaluation

- Authors: Tashenova, Zhuldyz; Aitmagambetuly, Aisultan; Urynbassarova, Altyn; Zhetkerbay, Askhat; Amanzholova, Shirin; Kerim, Akerke
- Year / venue: 2026, Big Data and Cognitive Computing (published)
- DOI: 10.3390/bdcc10090303 · URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/bdcc10090303
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)

Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.

## 1. Research objective
[A] To test whether high accuracies reported for learning-based detectors on synthetic corpora and random splits (including the authors' own SentinelCMS, ~93% accuracy on 600 synthetic snippets) transfer to real, disclosed WordPress plugin vulnerabilities. The second aim is to quantify how much duplicate leakage, contradictory labels and in-sample stacking inflated the authors' own first release (p. 2). The paper is a self-correcting re-evaluation prompted by an audit of the first release (p. 2; acknowledgment p. 14).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- [A] RQ1 (transfer): does training on real CVE data beat training on synthetic data? (p. 2)
- [A] RQ2 (detector families): how do static, classical and neural detectors compare under duplicate-controlled evaluation? (p. 2)
- [A] RQ3 (negatives and granularity): how do the negative-sampling variant and label granularity affect results? (p. 2)
- [A] RQ4 (evaluation validity): how much do duplicate leakage and in-sample stacking inflate reported performance? (p. 2)
- No formal hypotheses are stated.

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: [V] Benchmark construction plus a comparative evaluation of ten detector configurations under plugin-grouped five-fold cross-validation on complete held-out folds (p. 1, p. 5–6).
- Approach / model / intervention:
  - [V] **Static analysis (SAST arm):** a "two-pass intra-procedural analyzer" that propagates taint from user-controlled sources to security-sensitive sinks without sanitisation (p. 5). It is **not named and no version is given**; it is not an established tool such as Pixy, RIPS, Psalm/Phan taint mode, Semgrep or CodeQL. [I] It is most likely the taint component of the authors' own SentinelCMS (p. 2), but the paper does not say so. The authors call it "intra-procedural and lexical" (p. 13).
  - [V] **Classical ML:** Random Forest and linear SVM on character 2–4-gram TF-IDF (char_wb, max_features 5000) (p. 5–6).
  - [V] **Neural:** Bi-LSTM with attention, a unidirectional LSTM ablation, and a "combined" model that concatenates the taint verdict to the Bi-LSTM representation (p. 5).
  - [V] **Stacking:** logistic-regression meta-learner, in an in-sample form (the original buggy implementation, kept only to measure bias) and a nested out-of-fold form (the citable one). The LSTM tower is omitted from both (p. 5–6).
  - [V] **No LLMs and no pre-trained transformers were run.** CodeBERT was not run "because the transformers library is not installed in the evaluation environment and the host has no GPU" (p. 13). LLMs appear only in related work (p. 3).
- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] Three deliberately trivial baselines (p. 5):
  - majority class (always predicts the most frequent training class);
  - a source/sink presence rule (the same rule used for label cleaning);
  - a one-feature logistic regression on function token count.
  - [V] RQ1 also compares a Bi-LSTM trained on the 600-snippet synthetic corpus with real-to-real CV (p. 7).

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): [V] NVD CVE API v2 and CVEProject/cvelistV5. 6666 unique indexed CVE records; 1757 CVEs in 1281 plugins could be resolved to downloadable pre-fix/post-fix source pairs (p. 3). About 54% of indexed CVEs were unrecoverable because old releases/SVN tags were pruned (p. 3).
- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] PHP functions. 30,860 snippets per variant before de-duplication; 15,294 (Variant A) and 24,917 (Variant B) after leakage control (p. 5, Table 2).
  - **Class balance / prevalence:**
    - [V] Variant A: Safe/XSS/SQLi/RCE = 3895/8446/2104/849 (p. 5, Table 2), so vulnerable is the majority class; the majority baseline accuracy is 0.745 (p. 9).
    - [V] Variant B: 13,396/8531/2142/848 (p. 5, Table 2); majority baseline accuracy 0.538 (p. 8, Table 6).
    - [I] Vulnerable prevalence is therefore 74.5% (A) and 46.2% (B) (our calculation from Table 2 counts). Both are far above realistic prevalence because negatives are drawn per CVE.
  - [V] Test folds are complete and prevalence-preserving; no balancing or subsampling of test folds (p. 6).
- Sampling / selection method: [V] Labels come from tree-sitter diffs of vulnerable vs patched versions (p. 3):
  - functions touched by the fix are positives and receive the CVE's vulnerability type; untouched functions are negatives;
  - Variant A uses the patched twin as the negative; Variant B uses unmodified functions from the same plugin.
- Leakage control: [V] An audit of the first release found (p. 4, Table 1):
  - duplicate groups crossing folds: 166 groups / 1086 records (A) and 151 / 676 (B);
  - contradictory-label groups: 730 / 456 (1852 / 1199 records).
  - [V] Three corrections were applied (p. 4):
    - all conflicting-label hash groups were removed;
    - exact duplicates (SHA-256 of whitespace-normalised code) were merged;
    - near-duplicates were grouped into clone families (MinHash over 5-token shingles, Jaccard ≥ 0.9; AST node-type sequences, Jaccard ≥ 0.9) and each family was collapsed to one record.
  - [V] Grouping by connected components was rejected because one giant component covered 59.4% (A) / 72.1% (B) of the corpus (p. 4).
  - [V] Final folds share 0 hashes, 0 clone families and 0 plugins (p. 5, Table 2). Collapsing removed 50.4% of Variant A and 19.3% of Variant B (p. 5).
  - [V] There is no temporal split; all CVEs predate the experiments and no date cut-off is applied (pp. 3–6). [I] Temporal leakage is not addressed; it is less relevant here because no pre-trained model is used.
- Label quality: [V] A stratified 400-function expert review (single annotator, blind to the automated verdict) found (p. 11, Table 10):
  - HIGH tier precision 73.0% (27/37);
  - MEDIUM tier 44.7% (97/217);
  - LOW (discarded) tier 0.7% (1/146);
  - cleaned subset (HIGH+MEDIUM) 48.8% (124/254).
- Data availability (public? link?): [V] Labels, metadata, hashes, folds and a loader script are on GitHub (Aisultan05/wordpress-cve-benchmark) and Zenodo; the audited rebuild is release v2.1.0. Plugin source is not redistributed but reconstructed from WordPress.org (p. 14). [V] A 125-vulnerability / 247-safe expert-verified subset is released (p. 11).

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools:
  - [V] Splits and losses: StratifiedGroupKFold (scikit-learn 1.8.0), 5 folds, seed 42, grouped by plugin slug; class-weighted cross-entropy (p. 6, Table 3).
  - [V] LSTM settings (p. 6, Table 3):
    - sequence length 128, 40 epochs, embedding 64, hidden 128, 2 layers, dropout 0.3, batch 16, Adam lr 1e-3;
    - at most 4000 training records per fold; CPU only.
  - [V] RF: 300 trees, balanced class weights. LinearSVC: C 1.0, balanced (p. 6).
  - [V] Software: Python 3.14, PyTorch 2.11 (CPU), NumPy 2.4, tree-sitter-php (p. 7).
  - [V] The 128-token bound was chosen for tractability, not tuned; its effect is unmeasured (p. 6).
  - [V] Granularities: binary, three-class (Safe/SQLi/XSS) and four-class (+RCE), crossed with the two variants, giving six settings (p. 6).
  - [V] Result files are keyed to SHA-256 fingerprints of the dataset index and fold file (p. 6).
- Code availability: [V] Data, folds, per-fold predictions, scores and fingerprinted results are released (p. 1, p. 14). [I] Whether training code is in the same repository is implied ("released training scripts", p. 6) but the repository was not inspected.

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
  - [V] Macro-F1 is the headline metric (fold mean ± SD, 95% CI with t, 4 df) (p. 6).
  - [V] Also reported: accuracy, per-class precision/recall/F1, vulnerable-class recall and FNR, balanced accuracy, MCC and PR-AUC (p. 6).
  - [A] Accuracy is not comparable with the earlier release because collapsing changed the majority class; macro-F1, balanced accuracy and MCC should be used instead (p. 5, Table 2 note).
  - [V] **Vulnerable-class F1 alone is not reported for most models** (only per-class F1 for the Variant B four-class setting, p. 9, Table 7). [I] Headline numbers are therefore not directly comparable with the vulnerable-class F1 used by most studies in our corpus.
- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals):
  - [V] Paired tests across folds and across plugins, with Cohen's d; the plugin-level test is "the better-powered" (p. 6).
  - [V] Only one test result is reported in the text: RF vs majority on Variant A macro-F1 is significant across folds but not across plugins (Wilcoxon p = 0.295, d = 0.057) (p. 9).
  - [V] 95% CIs are reported for Variant B binary (p. 8, Table 6).
  - [V] No multiple-comparison correction is mentioned (pp. 6–9).

## 7. Key findings
1. **Overall detector ranking (RQ2)** — [V] Best macro-F1 is 0.563 (Variant A binary, SVM) and 0.601 (Variant B binary, nested stacking) (p. 7–8, Table 5). No neural configuration leads in any of the six settings; the gap to the best classical model is 2.1–6.4 pp (p. 8).
2. **Variant B binary in detail** — [V] Macro-F1 (95% CI) / MCC / vulnerable FNR / PR-AUC (p. 8, Table 6):

   | Detector | Macro-F1 (95% CI) | Bal. acc. | MCC | Vuln. FNR | PR-AUC |
   |---|---|---|---|---|---|
   | Nested stacking | 0.601 (0.579–0.624) | 0.601 | 0.203 | 0.455 | 0.590 |
   | RF + TF-IDF | 0.586 (0.574–0.598) | 0.594 | 0.203 | 0.593 | 0.600 |
   | uni-LSTM | 0.578 (0.563–0.594) | 0.584 | 0.168 | 0.401 | 0.555 |
   | Bi-LSTM | 0.573 (0.550–0.595) | 0.581 | 0.162 | 0.356 | 0.558 |
   | Function-length baseline | 0.572 (0.551–0.593) | 0.582 | 0.177 | 0.610 | 0.575 |
   | Combined taint + Bi-LSTM | 0.569 (0.530–0.609) | 0.579 | 0.157 | 0.425 | 0.552 |
   | SVM + TF-IDF | 0.562 (0.526–0.599) | 0.565 | 0.135 | 0.560 | 0.542 |
   | Source/sink rule | 0.480 (0.446–0.515) | 0.524 | 0.063 | 0.796 | 0.476 |
   | Static taint analyser | 0.366 (0.360–0.373) | 0.504 | 0.035 | 0.982 | 0.465 |
   | Majority baseline | 0.350 (0.349–0.350) | 0.500 | 0.000 | 1.000 | 0.462 |

   [V] Per-tool precision and recall for the vulnerable class are not reported separately; vulnerable recall = 1 − FNR (p. 8, Table 6).

3. **Static taint analyser (the only SAST arm)** — [V] Macro-F1 across the six settings: 0.221 / 0.160 / 0.116 (Variant A binary / 3-class / 4-class) and 0.366 / 0.256 / 0.188 (Variant B) (p. 8, Table 5). [V] It detects 1.7–1.8% of vulnerabilities (p. 9); vulnerable FNR is 0.982 on Variant B binary (p. 8, Table 6). [V] On Variant A binary its macro-F1 (0.221) is below the majority baseline (0.427) (p. 8, Table 5). [A] The low recall "reflects that implementation rather than taint analysis in general" (p. 13).
4. **Trivial baselines are hard to beat** — [V] The token-count baseline matches or exceeds the TF-IDF RF in four of six settings and is within 0.001 of the Bi-LSTM on Variant B binary (0.572 vs 0.573) (p. 8). [V] The source/sink rule's MCC is −0.001 to 0.063 (p. 8). [A] "Much of what the models exploit is correlated with function size rather than with security-relevant structure" (p. 8).
5. **Degenerate predictors hidden by aggregate scores** — [V] On Variant A the RF labels 15,068 of 15,294 records vulnerable (Safe recall 0.032); its accuracy 0.747 exceeds the majority baseline's 0.745 by 0.15 pp (p. 9). [V] On Variant B the same RF has a vulnerable-class FNR of 0.84–0.87 (p. 9). [V] Several models almost never predict RCE: RF RCE F1 0.000, uni-LSTM 0.002 (p. 9, Table 7).
6. **Synthetic vs real training (RQ1)** — [V] Real-to-real Bi-LSTM beats synthetic-to-real only in binary settings (+0.034 and +0.078 macro-F1); in four-class settings synthetic is marginally ahead (−0.019, −0.017) (p. 7, Table 4).
7. **In-sample stacking bias (RQ4)** — [V] Mean +1.27 pp macro-F1; optimistic in 5 of 6 settings (max +2.95 pp) but −1.62 pp in Variant B binary (p. 10, Table 8). [V] Duplicate leakage is not expressed as a single number; before correction 1086 / 676 test records were exact copies of training material (p. 10).
8. **Label cleaning confounded** — [V] Restricting to source-to-sink functions raises Variant A 3-class macro-F1 by +0.112 to +0.222 for learned models but only +0.009 to +0.013 on Variant B binary; the taint analyser gains +0.129 / +0.085 (p. 10, Table 9). [A] The filtered subset is easier as well as cleaner, so cleaning is "a plausible but unproven lever" (p. 10).
9. **Label quality** — [V] 48.8% of cleaned positive labels are genuine vulnerabilities (124/254); the discarded LOW tier is 0.7% genuine (p. 11, Table 10). [V] Only 0.3% of discarded pairs contain a genuine inter-procedural source-to-sink path; 71% contain no taint source at all (p. 12).
10. **Comparison with prior work** — [V] Prior PHP detector DeepTective reported F1 0.881 on a random split vs this work's best macro-F1 0.601 (plugin-grouped, de-duplicated) (p. 12, Table 12). [A] The gap is "best explained by methodology rather than model quality" (p. 12).
11. **Trivial-baseline comparison** — [I] Our calculation from Table 2 counts (p. 5):
    - Variant B binary (46.2% vulnerable): an always-vulnerable predictor would score vulnerable-class F1 ≈ 0.632 and macro-F1 ≈ 0.316. The reported majority (always-Safe) baseline is 0.350 (p. 8).
    - Variant A binary (74.5% vulnerable): the majority baseline *is* always-vulnerable, at macro-F1 0.427 (p. 8, Table 5).
    - The best detectors exceed these trivial levels by about 0.14–0.25 macro-F1, with MCC ≤ 0.203 (p. 8, Table 6). The 0.667 balanced-data reference does not apply, because neither variant is balanced and the metric is macro-F1.

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] The protocol is "duplicate-controlled rather than provably leakage-free"; semantic clones that differ lexically and structurally may persist (p. 13).
- [A] About 54% of indexed CVEs were unrecoverable, so the corpus may be biased toward plugins that retain historical versions (p. 13).
- [A] Rare-class estimates are unreliable (RCE 848 records in Variant B; several models never predict it); four-class results are indicative only (p. 13).
- [A] Neural models trained on ≤4000 records/fold for 40 epochs on CPU, so their numbers are a lower bound (p. 13).
- [A] No transformer comparison (CodeBERT not run; no GPU); the 256-token sensitivity run is outstanding (p. 13).
- [A] The taint analyser is intra-procedural and lexical (p. 13).
- [A] Labels are only about half correct on the positive class, which "bounds what any model trained on them can demonstrate" (p. 13).
- [A] The expert sample was labelled by a single annotator, so no inter-annotator agreement is reported (p. 11).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] **The SAST arm is a weak straw-man for our RQ1.** It is an unnamed in-house intra-procedural lexical analyser (p. 5, p. 13). No established PHP SAST tool (e.g. Psalm taint analysis, Semgrep, RIPS/Pixy descendants, CodeQL — which does not support PHP) was run. The "misses about 98%" result cannot be generalised to PHP SAST.
- [I] **No LLM arm at all** (p. 3, p. 13). For our review the paper informs SAST-vs-DL and evaluation methodology, not LLM-vs-anything.
- [I] **Label precision of the main benchmark is not reported.** The 48.8% figure (p. 11) refers to the cleaned HIGH+MEDIUM subset. The main experiments (Tables 5–6) use the full corpus, which also contains LOW-tier functions found 0.7% genuine (p. 11) and the 13,702 "noisy" discarded pairs (p. 11, Table 11). Genuine-positive precision in the evaluated corpus is therefore plausibly well below 48.8%, but is not reported. This makes every absolute score hard to interpret.
- [I] **Macro-F1 headline** mixes Safe-class and vulnerable-class F1. Combined with class proportions that differ between variants (74.5% vs 46.2% vulnerable), this makes cross-variant and cross-paper comparisons fragile.
- [I] **Function-level granularity, not repository-level.** It does not test inter-procedural or cross-file detection, which is the core of our G5 interest. The inter-procedural recovery experiment found only 39 paths (p. 11).
- [I] **Self-correction context.** The paper corrects the authors' own earlier release after reviewers audited the artifacts (p. 2, p. 14). This is commendable transparency, but it also means the earlier SentinelCMS numbers (~93%, p. 2) should not be cited.
- [I] **Minor presentation issues:**
  - The statements are in the singular ("The author declares", "The author thanks") for a six-author paper (p. 14).
  - Only one significance test is actually reported despite paired tests being described (p. 6, p. 9).
- [I] **No negatives from unrelated code at realistic prevalence.** Both variants draw negatives from vulnerable plugins only, so the deployment false-alarm rate is unknown.

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection):
  - [V] Strong exact- and near-duplicate control with verified 0/0/0 cross-fold overlap (p. 5).
  - [V] In-sample stacking leakage is measured and corrected (p. 10).
  - [A] Semantic clones may remain (p. 13).
  - [I] Label noise (≤48.8% genuine positives) is the dominant confound. Diff-based labelling marks every function touched by a fix as vulnerable, including non-security edits (p. 4, p. 11).
  - [V] The filtered-subset comparison is confounded by easier test cases (p. 10).
- External (generalisability of sample/context):
  - [V] WordPress plugins only, PHP only, XSS/SQLi/RCE only (p. 5).
  - [A] Survivorship bias toward plugins with retained history (p. 13).
  - [I] Results may not transfer to other PHP frameworks (Laravel, Drupal) or to repository-level detection.
- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?):
  - [I] Macro-F1 averages a Safe-class F1 that depends heavily on negative sampling (Variant A vs B).
  - [I] Labels measure "touched by a security fix" more than "vulnerable".
  - [V] The per-class tables expose degenerate predictors that aggregate scores hide (p. 9).
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance):
  - [V] 5 folds give only five paired observations; a plugin-level test is used as the better-powered alternative (p. 6).
  - [V] CIs are reported for Variant B binary only (p. 8).
  - [V] No multiple-comparison correction is reported (pp. 6–10).
  - [V] A single seed (42) is used throughout (p. 7).
  - [I] Many between-model gaps (e.g. 0.562–0.601 on Variant B binary) have overlapping CIs (p. 8, Table 6).
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [V] Good — hyper-parameters (p. 6–7), folds, per-fold predictions, fingerprinted results and a loader script are released (p. 14). Plugin code must be re-downloaded from WordPress.org (p. 14). [I] Reproducibility therefore depends on WordPress.org continuing to host old versions, the same pruning that already lost 54% of CVEs (p. 3).

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A]:
  - extend expert review to several thousand functions with ≥2 annotators and adjudication, and evaluate on an expert-verified test set (p. 13);
  - use curated feeds that name entry points and sinks (p. 13);
  - semantic clone detection (p. 13);
  - a fully resourced transformer comparison on identical folds and a 256-token sensitivity run (p. 13);
  - require future detectors to clear trivial baselines such as function length (p. 13).
- Suggested by us [I]:
  - Run established PHP SAST tools (Semgrep PHP rules, Psalm taint mode, Progpilot) and 1–2 open LLMs on the released expert-verified 125/247 subset (p. 11). That would give a small but clean PHP LLM-vs-SAST-vs-ML comparison, directly addressing G5 and G2.
  - Report vulnerable-class F1 and precision at realistic prevalence alongside macro-F1.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ2 (primary), RQ1 (SAST vs ML/DL only; no LLM), RQ4 (PHP; per-CWE-class behaviour), RQ5.
- How it informs our work [I]:
  - **RQ2:** a clean demonstration that duplicate leakage, contradictory labels, in-sample stacking and label noise shape measured performance more than model family. It is also a second study (beside shu2026evaluating) that reports trivial baselines and finds they are competitive, which strengthens G1.
  - **G5 (PHP):** gives real-CVE PHP evidence, but at function level and without LLMs or a standard SAST tool. G5 therefore remains open, but the released corpus and expert-verified subset are a ready data source for the G5 study.
  - **G2:** the closest PHP analogue to a leakage-controlled same-benchmark comparison, missing the LLM arm.
  - **RQ4:** XSS is detected far better than RCE by learned models (p. 9), and SQLi per-class F1 is ≤ 0.146 (p. 9, Table 7). This is a hint that rare classes are effectively undetected by small ML models on PHP.
  - **C5 (class balance):** the choice of negatives flips the majority class and the failure direction of the same RF model (p. 9).

content.content:
## 7. Key findings
1. In-distribution DL (within-dataset) — [V] LineVul F1 94.52 and VulBERTa 94.14 on Juliet; LineVul F1 91.00 on BigVul (p. 11; Table 6 p. 12). On BigVul, ReVeal, Devign and VulBERTa reach accuracy 87.45, 94.09, 94.39 but F1 only 23.58, 16.90, 0.19 (p. 11). [A] Because BigVul has a much smaller vulnerable share (6%), "predictions biased toward the non-vulnerable majority class can produce high accuracy while detecting few vulnerable functions" (p. 11).
2. Cross-dataset DL — [V] LineVul (Juliet) F1 94.52 in-dataset falls to 53.95 (Devign), 10.73 (BigVul), 51.22 (ICVul) (p. 11). LineVul (BigVul) falls from 91.00 to 0 (Juliet), 1.90 (Devign), 13.05 (ICVul) (p. 12). ReVeal (BigVul) is below 1.00 F1 on all three external sets (p. 11). [A] "No evaluated model consistently preserves its within-dataset performance" (p. 11).
3. Temporally separated DL (VentiVul, Whole-File) — [V] F1 3.47–8.65 across the 8 ReVeal/LineVul configurations; best ReVeal (BigVul) F1 8.65 with precision 5.25%, recall 24.43% (p. 13, Table 7). Devign-trained models: recall 99.24–100% but precision about 2% (p. 13, Table 7). LineVul (BigVul) F1 6.87 on VentiVul vs 91.00 in-distribution (Table 7 p. 13; Table 6 p. 12).
4. Temporally separated LLMs (VentiVul) — [V] Conservative F1 0.79–5.36 across 4 models × 3 prompts; all conservative F1 < 5.5% and all PACC < 6% (p. 13; Table 8 p. 14). Best: Mistral-Small-24B few-shot F1 5.36%, CDR 46%, PACC 5.75% (p. 13). Highest valid-only F1: Qwen2.5-Coder-32B CoT 8.21% (conservative 3.04%) (p. 14, Table 8). Zero-shot conservative F1: Qwen2.5-Coder 3.72, DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite 4.29, Qwen3 3.09, Mistral 4.07 (p. 14, Table 8). LLM precision and recall are not reported, and the LLMs have no in-distribution numbers.
5. DL vs LLM on VentiVul (mostly but not exactly the same samples) [V/I] — [V] best DL Whole-File F1 8.65 (ReVeal-BigVul) vs best LLM conservative F1 5.36 (Mistral few-shot) (p. 13; p. 14). Zero-shot LLM CDR (34%, 20%, 9%, 5%) is lower than most DL configurations (p. 13). Best PACC: DL 5.34% vs LLM 5.75% (p. 13). [V] The evaluated samples differ: ReVeal is scored only on functions it can process (p. 7), the few-shot test set excludes pairs used as demonstrations, and valid-only metrics use only parseable outputs (p. 8). [I] F1 against chance (all-positive F1 ≈ 3.87% at p = 1.97%; ≈ 3.5% on ReVeal's subset; §4): the best DL F1 of 8.65 is about 2.5× its chance level, while the best LLM F1 of 5.36 is about 1.4× chance. LineVul (Devign), with recall 100%, precision 2% and F1 3.93, is in effect the all-positive predictor (p. 13, Table 7). [I] PACC against chance: a random labeller that flags a fraction q of functions independently of their content would get PACC = q(1−q), up to 25% at q = 0.5. All observed PACC values (≤ 5.75%, DL and LLM) are far below that, which means the models usually give the vulnerable and the patched version the same label (our reasoning from the PACC definition, p. 9). This matches ding2025vulnerability, where random pair-wise correctness is 22.70% and models fall far below it [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9].
6. CDR vs PACC gap — [V] ReVeal (Devign), ReVeal (ICVul), LineVul (Devign) reach CDR 99.10%, 94.59%, 100% but PACC 0.76%, 0%, 0% (p. 13). [A] Detecting a vulnerable function "does not imply" telling it apart from its patch (p. 13).
7. Prompting — [V] Few-shot improves Mistral on all three metrics but degrades the other models; CoT raises Qwen2.5-Coder valid-only F1 but lowers its PACC (p. 13). [A] Prompting effects are "model- and metric-dependent" (p. 13).
8. Project/CWE variation — [V] All LLMs have higher CDR on Linux than Chromium. DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite zero-shot CDR is 26% on Chromium and 42% on Linux (p. 13). LineVul (BigVul) has CDR 76% on Chromium and 0 on Linux (p. 13). The LLM project-specific results are zero-shot, valid-only (p. 13). Best project-specific PACC is < 8% (LineVul-ICVul 7.48% on Chromium) (p. 14). Per-CWE PACC peaks at 18.18% (LineVul-ICVul, CWE-472) on small cells (p. 14).
9. Representations — [V] GNN centroid distances: Juliet 0.0242, ICVul 0.0057, BigVul 0.1612; CodeBERT: BigVul 0.166, Devign 0.0068 (pp. 9–10). [A] Neither representation consistently separates vulnerable from non-vulnerable code (p. 10).

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] Only four DL models, two DL families on VentiVul, four open-weight LLMs; no proprietary LLMs; conclusions apply to the evaluated models (p. 17).
- [A] LLM pretraining corpora and cutoffs are unknown, so temporal separation "cannot fully exclude training-data contamination" (p. 17).
- [A] t-SNE is parameter-sensitive, and centroid distance cannot capture nonlinear structure. RQ1 does not establish a causal link to RQ2/RQ3 performance (p. 17, p. 15).
- [A] Dataset characteristics vary simultaneously, so individual causes cannot be isolated. Preprocessing drops some functions, which affects comparability (p. 17).
- [A] VentiVul is C/C++ only (Linux, Chromium) and may not generalise to other languages or proprietary code. "Unrelated" functions may hide other vulnerabilities (residual label noise), and regex function extraction can miss complex C/C++ syntax, which mainly affects Whole-File (p. 17).
- [A] VentiVul "does not contain every vulnerability reported for the selected project versions" (incomplete coverage) (p. 17).
- [A] Model coverage was constrained by reproducibility, experimental consistency and computational feasibility; conclusions apply "to the evaluated models and settings rather than to all existing vulnerability detection techniques" (p. 17).
- [A] The Function-Pair setting is "less exposed" to label-noise and extraction threats because it uses manually verified vulnerable functions and their patched versions (p. 17).
- [A] ICVul and VentiVul come from open-source projects and may not represent proprietary industrial software (p. 17).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] No trivial baseline. At p = 263/13,326 = 1.97% (p. 4), an all-positive classifier scores F1 = 2p/(1+p) ≈ 3.87%. All eight DL F1 values (3.47–8.65, Table 7 p. 13) are at most 4.8 points above that. Seven of the 12 LLM conservative F1 values (Table 8 p. 14) fall below it: 3.72, 2.95, 3.04, 3.64, 3.09, 0.79 and 1.39. The paper calls these results "limited" or "weak" (p. 13) but never compares them with chance.
- [I] The DL and LLM comparison is asymmetric. DL models were trained on historical data; LLMs were used zero/few-shot without fine-tuning, with small open-weight models (MoE models with 2.4–3B active parameters) and Qwen3 thinking disabled (p. 5, p. 8). The study says nothing about frontier or fine-tuned LLMs, and nothing about LLMs in-distribution, because LLMs were not run on the four benchmarks.
- [I] LLM precision/recall are not reported (Table 8 gives F1, CDR, PACC only, p. 14), so we cannot tell whether LLMs fail through false positives or false negatives.
- [I] No confidence intervals. LLMs get a single deterministic run (temperature 0, seed 42, p. 8); DL run counts and seeds are not reported. With 263 pairs, PACC differences of a few points (e.g. 5.34% vs 5.75%) are within noise.
- [I] One function at a time with no context (p. 7). This is fair between families but disadvantages LLMs, which may need inter-procedural context. With 263 pairs across 200 CVEs (p. 4), at most 63 CVEs have more than one affected function (e.g. CVE-2025-37777, two functions in two files, p. 4). The share of CVEs that need cross-function reasoning is not reported.
- [I] No static-analysis tool is evaluated, although the introduction positions learning-based detection as a complement to static analysis (p. 1).
- [I] Version: we analyse arXiv v4 (4 Nov 2026), the accepted manuscript (footnote p. 1). The published JSS version (doi 10.1016/j.jss.2026.113185, Crossref-verified 2026-11-12) is not open access and was not compared with it, so small differences between the two versions cannot be ruled out. Page refs follow arXiv v4.

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal: [I] Deduplication within datasets and fixed test sets are reported (p. 7), but split ratios and cross-dataset overlap checks are not reported (Devign is from FFmpeg/QEMU and BigVul from open-source C/C++ repositories, p. 3, so project overlap is possible but unchecked). ReVeal is scored only on functions it can process (p. 7), which may inflate or deflate its numbers relative to LineVul. Overlap with training and pretraining data was not checked. Temporal separation covers the CVEs and their fixes (disclosed from May 2025, p. 4). The "unrelated" same-file functions that make up most of VentiVul can be much older code. The paper describes BigVul and ICVul only as drawn from open-source C/C++ repositories and GitHub fix commits (p. 3), and does not say whether they contain older Linux/Chromium code. It reports no check of whether VentiVul functions appear in the DL training sets or in LLM pretraining corpora (pp. 3–4).
- Conflict of interest: [I] ICVul, one of the four training benchmarks, is the authors' own dataset (Lu, Li, Dehaene, Lagaisse, MSR 2025; p. 3, reference list p. 18). The paper presents it as "high-quality" (p. 3). Its results are not singled out favourably, but the dependence should be noted. Funding: not reported (no funding or acknowledgement statement in the text).
- External: [I] C/C++, two very large projects, 200 CVEs, open-weight mid-size LLMs only (p. 4, p. 5).
- Construct: [I] Labelling unrelated same-file functions as non-vulnerable (p. 4) is a realistic construct for "scan the whole file", though label noise remains (p. 17). PACC is a strict and useful measure of patch sensitivity. CDR rewards indiscriminate positive prediction, as the paper itself shows (p. 13).
- Statistical conclusion: [I] No tests, single runs, small per-CWE cells (p. 14).
- Reproducibility: [I] Good overall: data, code and results are public (p. 2), and the decoding settings are fully given (p. 8). Prompt templates are given (Table 4, p. 9), but the system prompt is only paraphrased (p. 8) and the few-shot demonstrations are not listed in the paper. DL hyper-parameters are given only by reference to the original implementations (p. 8), and DL run counts and seeds are not reported.

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A]: representations and training that emphasise security-relevant changes, e.g. vulnerable–patched pair supervision (p. 16); datasets prioritising reliable labels, diverse patterns and explicit vulnerability–fix links over size (p. 16); complementing within-dataset evaluation with cross-dataset and temporally separated testing, and reporting CDR and patch-pair metrics with function-level metrics (p. 16); studying individual dataset factors, broader ecosystems and "more advanced LLM adaptation strategies" (p. 16).
- Suggested by us [I]: run SAST tools and frontier/fine-tuned LLMs on VentiVul with file/repository context and a chance baseline. That would give exactly the same-benchmark LLM vs SAST vs DL comparison our RQ5 identifies as missing.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1 (DL vs LLM on largely shared OOD data), RQ2 (temporal separation, cross-dataset shift, class ratio, accuracy vs F1), RQ4 (per-project and per-CWE variation, C/C++), RQ5 (patch-pair sensitivity, chance baselines).
- How it informs our work [I]: This is direct, peer-reviewed (JSS 2026) evidence that in-distribution DL scores do not survive temporal shift. It is consistent with ding2025vulnerability, which shows BigVul-trained models collapse on PrimeVul [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7]. LineVul's F1 falls from 91–94.5 in-distribution (p. 12) to 4.39–6.87 on VentiVul, and all 8 DL configurations score 3.47–8.65 (p. 13). On F1, the evaluated open-weight LLMs (≤ 32B) do no better than the shifted DL detectors (0.79–5.36), and both families sit within a few points of the all-positive F1 of ≈ 3.87%. On PACC, both families are far below the random q(1−q) level (up to 25%), i.e. they rarely tell a function apart from its patch. It supports the RQ2 claim that evaluation setup drives the reported ranking. It covers no SAST tool or cost, so it adds nothing for RQ3.

- Authors: Qin, Letong
- Year / venue: 2026, Computers and Artificial Intelligence (published) — **venue flag [I]:** published by Zeus Press (p. 1); no peer-review statement or received/accepted dates in the PDF (pp. 1–16); low-visibility source not in DOAJ (OpenAlex, 2026-11-12). Peer review is not documented; weight like grey literature (see Analyst notes).
- DOI: 10.70267/cai.v3n5.122137 · URL: https://doi.org/10.70267/cai.v3n5.122137
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)

Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.

## 1. Research objective
- [A] Review source-code vulnerability detection with "lightweight code Transformers and large-scale language models" as the two lines of discussion, covering input construction, task adaptation, use of program-analysis information and multi-model collaboration, and compare them by datasets, metrics and deployment conditions (p. 1).
- [A] Scope is limited to source-code-level detection, localization and classification; network intrusion, malware, smart contracts, vulnerability generation and automatic repair are excluded (p. 1).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- [A] Three organising questions in the introduction: what capabilities methods actually improve, under what data conditions/protocols the gains are obtained, and whether evidence suffices for real-world deployment (p. 2).
- [A] Four formal RQs: RQ1 development from sequence/graph models to code pretraining and LLM interaction; RQ2 performance evidence of direct prompting, in-context learning, fine-tuning, structural enhancement and multi-model collaboration; RQ3 effects of label noise, duplication, class imbalance and temporal leakage; RQ4 how cross-project, out-of-time, false-positive-cost, localization and explanation evaluation approach deployment (p. 4).
- [I] The two framings are not reconciled: the introduction organises the paper around "three closely related questions" (p. 2), while Section 3.1 sets four formal RQs (p. 4), and the paper does not map one onto the other. Separately, it gives "medium confidence to C2" (p. 12), but no claim labelled C1/C2 is defined anywhere in the text.

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: [I] Narrative (traditional) review. The paper calls itself a "review" (p. 1) and gives no search strategy, databases, search strings, date window, inclusion/exclusion screening, PRISMA flow, or study-quality assessment — all "not reported". The only inclusion rule stated is that it "includes only studies that directly analyze source code" and excludes repair (p. 4).
- Approach / taxonomy: [A] Methods are classified "by how vulnerability knowledge is acquired" rather than by model scale, core technology or supply-chain stage as in earlier reviews (p. 4). Two routes: (a) lightweight code Transformers — code pretraining + supervised fine-tuning, input granularity, structural fusion (pp. 5–6); (b) large-scale LLMs — supervised fine-tuning/steering, multitask learning, direct prompting, few-shot/ICL, hybrid detection with program analysis, ensembles/multi-model collaboration, explanation (pp. 6–9). Figure 1 adds cross-cutting layers "Data and bias", "Reliability evaluation" and "Discussion and outlook" (p. 3) [V, from figure].
- Baselines or comparison conditions: [A] Traditional methods (SAST, GNNs) are discussed "only in two situations": to motivate structural information for Transformers and as baselines or external tools for LLMs; "this paper does not provide a separate review of traditional detection methods" (p. 4). Section 7.1 nevertheless compares LLMs with DL and SAST qualitatively (pp. 11–12).
## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] Not systematic: no search protocol, databases, screening, corpus count or quality assessment (absence across pp. 1–4). Its conclusions cannot be checked for selection bias, and it cannot be cited as a systematic review.
- [I] Small and selective corpus (32 references, pp. 14–16). Missing, among others, project-scale LLM/SAST studies and LLM-based SAST-alarm filtering work that we have (e.g. li2026llm, du2026reducing, xiong2026sifting, li2024iris, guo2025repoaudit); hybrid claims rest on GRACE, DLAP and one context-enhancement study (p. 8), not on SAST+LLM evaluations.
- [I] SAST is explicitly out of scope (p. 4), yet the review draws an LLM-vs-SAST conclusion (p. 12) from two references [1, 15] with no numbers. Only [15] compares the two families, and it favours LLMs on F1 [@gnieciak2025large, p. 10]. That conclusion is under-supported.
- [I] Contradictions are explained only in general terms. Apart from the PrimeVul Table V re-reading (p. 12), it does not tabulate conflicting results from different studies side by side against their evaluation setups (benchmark, split, class ratio, granularity). Table 1 (pp. 6–7) is qualitative: no numbers, no split type per study.
- [I] Cites PrimeVul as a 2024 arXiv preprint (p. 15) and leans heavily on that one study for the inflation argument.
- [I] Editorial loose ends (the three framing questions on p. 2 are not reconciled with the four formal RQs on p. 4; "C2" on p. 12 is undefined) suggest light editorial review (see Analyst notes on venue).

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal (selection): [I] Unknown selection process, so selection bias cannot be judged; the reviewer's framing (evaluation pitfalls) may have driven which studies were cited.
- External: [I] Mostly C/C++ function-level benchmarks (BigVul, PrimeVul, DiverseVul, SeVC, ReVeal, FFmpeg+Qemu; pp. 8–9, 12); multilingual evidence is one reference [32] (p. 13).
- Source dependence: [I] Its quantitative claims rest on a handful of cited studies, mainly PrimeVul [14] for benchmark inflation (pp. 2, 12) and Gnieciak & Szandala [15] for LLM vs SAST (p. 12). Both are already in our corpus (ding2025vulnerability, gnieciak2025large). Counting this review as extra support for the same claims would double-count them.
- Construct: [I] Good conceptual separation of label correctness, localization and explanation evidence (p. 4); recommends metrics beyond F1 (p. 11).
- Statistical conclusion: [I] No quantitative synthesis; confidence levels ("medium confidence to C2", p. 12) are given without a stated grading scheme.
- Reproducibility: [I] Not reproducible as a review (no protocol, no study list beyond references).

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A]: traceable data pipelines with commit, time, label-source and duplicate statistics and updateable data cards (p. 13); out-of-time and project-isolated testing as main evidence, random splits only for historical comparison (p. 13); uncertainty calibration, risk-coverage curves and recall at a fixed false-positive budget (p. 13); decomposed verification of explanations (location, trigger, path, CWE, fix) (p. 13); human-machine studies recording audit time per real vulnerability (p. 13); SAST-LLM systems that measure candidate recall, LLM filtering gain, explanation correctness and total audit cost separately (p. 13); preserving system prompts, model IDs, call dates, temperatures and repetition counts (p. 13).
- Suggested by us [I]: a systematic, protocol-based review that puts SAST, DL and LLM results on the same evaluation-setup axes. This is exactly the gap between this review and ours.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ2 (primary), RQ3 (conceptual only), RQ1 (qualitative only), RQ5.
- How it informs our work [I]: This is the closest competing review and must be cited for positioning. Overlap: evaluation-reliability framing (duplicates, label noise, temporal splits, contamination) and the SAST-LLM-human workflow recommendation. Difference: it is narrative, has a small corpus (32 references), explicitly excludes SAST as a reviewed family, gives no quantitative LLM-vs-SAST or hybrid evidence, and does not map contradictions study-by-study onto evaluation setup. Our contribution should be stated against those four points. Its recommendations agree with our RQ2 answer, but they do not corroborate it independently: qin cites ding2025vulnerability [14], gnieciak2025large [15] and sheng2025llms [21] (p. 15), which are all in our corpus. Weak strength; use it for positioning only.

**Title:** "Evaluating LLMs for Real-World Web Vulnerability Detection"

**Authors:** Sebastian Neef, Luca Jungnickel, Antonio Benjamin Buchholz, Valene Spence, Vicente Birke Gonzalez

**Submission date:** 19 June 2026 (v1, arXiv:2606.21397, cs.CR)

**Comments field:** "To be published at AI&CCPS Workshop @ ARES 2026"

**Abstract (paraphrased):** I can't reproduce the full abstract verbatim, since that would exceed the 125-character limit on quoted material. In summary, the paper benchmarks six frontier and open-weight LLMs on detecting real-world web vulnerabilities in WordPress plugins, including SQL injection, stored XSS, path traversal, and remote code execution. The authors test five prompt designs across three experiment iterations. They find that all models can identify valid security issues, but detection rates vary by model and prompt. Claude Opus 4.6 had the highest detection rate at 63%, while the open-weight MiniMax M2.5 reached 48% and self-hosted Qwen 3.5 reached 35%. Scoped prompts that narrow the vulnerability focus outperformed open-ended ones, while prompt complexity had little effect. No model was fully consistent across the three iterations, and some were as low as 50%. No model correctly found one baseline vulnerability in one plugin. The authors also share practical lessons for security practitioners and publish their code and data.

You can read the full abstract on the arXiv page (arxiv.org/abs/2606.21397).

I can't reproduce the full abstract verbatim, because it's far longer than the 125-character limit on quoted text. Here are the other details:

- **Title:** "Are Frontier LLMs Ready for Cybersecurity? Evidence for Vertical Foundation Models from Dual-Mode Vulnerability Benchmarks"
- **Authors:** Vivek Dahiya, Sunny Nehra, Vipul Dholariya, Bhavik Shangari, Chandra Khatri
- **Submission date:** 22 May 2026 (v1). The current version, v5, was revised on 26 June 2026.
- **Comments field:** None appears on the page.

**Abstract summary:** The paper evaluates whether frontier LLMs are ready for cybersecurity work. It uses two benchmarks: one for detecting vulnerabilities in individual functions in C, Java, and Python code, and one for black-box security testing of five web applications with 118 known vulnerabilities. The authors test six frontier models and two domain-specialized models. They report high false-positive rates in code review, low coverage in web testing even with security tools added, and better detection when models follow structured penetration-testing methods. A specialized defense model had the best precision and lowest false-positive rate, and it ran on a single GPU. The authors identify a lack of realistic security-testing traces as the main training-data bottleneck, propose self-play as a way to generate that data, and argue for purpose-built cybersecurity models.

For the exact abstract, see the arXiv page at https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23243.

== 10.48550/arxiv.2503.01449 | Benchmarking Large Language Models for Multi-Language Software Vulnerability Detection | arXiv (Cornell University) 2025
Recent advancements in generative AI have led to the widespread adoption of large language models (LLMs) in software engineering, addressing numerous long-standing challenges. However, a comprehensive study examining the capabilities of LLMs in software vulnerability detection (SVD), a crucial aspect of software security, is currently lacking. Existing research primarily focuses on evaluating LLMs using C/C++ datasets. It typically explores only one or two strategies among prompt engineering, instruction tuning, and sequence classification fine-tuning for open-source LLMs. Consequently, there is a significant knowledge gap regarding the effectiveness of diverse LLMs in detecting vulnerabilities across various programming languages. To address this knowledge gap, we present a comprehensive empirical study evaluating the performance of LLMs on the SVD task. We have compiled a comprehensive dataset comprising 8,260 vulnerable functions in Python, 7,505 in Java, and 28,983 in JavaScript. We assess five open-source LLMs using multiple approaches, including prompt engineering, instruction tuning, and sequence classification fine-tuning. These LLMs are benchmarked against five fine-tuned small language models and two open-source static application security testing tools. Furthermore, we explore two avenues to improve LLM performance on SVD: a) Data perspective: Retraining models using downsampled balanced datasets. b) Model perspective: Investigating ensemble learning methods that c

== W7218261049 | A Comparative Evaluation of Large Language Models for Real-World Vulnerability Detection: An Empirical Study on Big-Vul and CVEfixes | International Journal of Advanced Natural Sciences and Engineering Researches 2026
Large language models are increasingly used in source code understanding, bug detection, and secure software development workflows. However, their effectiveness in vulnerability detection is often evaluated on synthetic benchmarks or short code snippets, leaving open questions about their reliability on real-world software artifacts. This study presents a comparative empirical evaluation of three large language models — GPT-4.1, GPT-4o, and Claude Sonnet 4.6 — on two real-world vulnerability datasets: Big-Vul and CVEfixes. The experiments evaluate zero-shot, few-shot, and structured chain-of-thought (CoT) prompts on balanced samples from both datasets and compare model performance against static analysis baselines. Strict F1 is used as the primary metric, treating parse failures as prediction errors. Probability-based metrics (AUC-ROC, AP) are also reported. On Big-Vul, Claude Sonnet 4.6 with structured CoT achieves the highest strict F1 of 0.574, whereas on CVEfixes, GPT-4.1 with structured CoT obtains the highest strict F1 of 0.667. However, AUC-ROC values remain between 0.49 and 0.56 across all Big-Vul configurations, indicating near-random confidence calibration despite higher F1 scores. McNemar tests show no statistically significant differences between model pairs on Big-Vul, while on CVEfixes, GPT-4.1 CoT significantly outperforms GPT-4o zero-shot after Bonferroni correction (p=0.0026). These findings indicate that large language models can provide useful vulnerability

== 10.66571/tsarka-3134-6057-11 | ON-PREMISE OPEN-WEIGHT LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS FOR INTERPRETABLE WEB VULNERABILITY DETECTION: A BENCHMARK AGAINST CLOUD MODELS AND RULE-BASED STATIC ANALYSIS | TSARKA Science 2026
Organisations handling regulated or proprietary source code are frequently prohibited from transmitting it to third-party inference providers, which excludes commercial cloud large language models from their security-analysis pipelines regardless of the accuracy those models achieve. Whether self-hosted open-weight models can substitute for them on ordinary developer hardware has not been established. This study benchmarks five quantised open-weight models, from 1.5 to 8 billion parameters and executed entirely on a consumer laptop graphics processor with eight gigabytes of video memory, on 120 annotated web-application code snippets spanning five weakness categories. Each was evaluated under zero-shot, few-shot and chain-of-thought prompting and compared against a rule-based static analyser and previously published cloud-model results on the identical corpus. The strongest local configuration reached an F1-score of 0.900, exceeding the previous-generation cloud flagship and trailing the current one by 4.7 points, while generating a remediation suggestion for every correct detection. The analysis further shows that F1 alone conceals degenerate behaviour: several configurations, including one cloud model, approach the score of a classifier labelling every input as vulnerable, so reporting specificity alongside F1 is proposed as a minimum requirement. Privacy-preserving on-premise vulnerability analysis is thus attainable without specialised infrastructure.

== 10.3390/e27090926 | Benchmarking Static Analysis for PHP Applications Security | Entropy 2025
PHP is the most widely used server-side programming language, but it remains highly susceptible to diverse classes of vulnerabilities. Static Application Security Testing (SAST) tools are commonly adopted for vulnerability detection; however, their evaluation lacks systematic criteria capable of quantifying information loss and uncertainty in analysis. Existing approaches, often based on small real-world case sets or heuristic sampling, fail to control experimental entropy within test cases. This uncontrolled variability makes it difficult to measure the information gain provided by different tools and to accurately differentiate their performance under varying levels of structural and semantic complexity. In this paper, we have developed a systematic evaluation framework for PHP SAST tools, designed to provide accurate and comprehensive assessments of their vulnerability detection capabilities. The framework explicitly isolates key factors influencing data flow analysis, enabling evaluation over four progressive dimensions with controlled information diversity. The paper is arXiv:2503.01449, submitted March 3, 2025 by Ting Zhang, Chengran Yang, and nine coauthors, including David Lo at Singapore Management University. It empirically evaluates various LLMs and adaptation strategies for software vulnerability detection across Python, Java, and JavaScript, and compares them with small language models and static application security testing tools.

- **Dataset:** The authors compiled 8,260 vulnerable functions in Python, 7,505 in Java, and 28,983 in JavaScript.
- **Models:** The study assesses five open-source LLMs using multiple approaches, including prompt engineering, instruction tuning, and sequence classification fine-tuning.
- **SAST comparison:** Two open-source SAST tools serve as the baseline. The paper reports that SAST tools consistently exhibit lower effectiveness compared to both LLMs and SLMs across all evaluated programming languages.
- **Overall findings:** The authors conclude that the relative effectiveness of LLMs versus SLMs in software vulnerability detection is programming language-dependent. They also state that SVD remains a challenging task for LLMs.
- **Improvement attempts:** The authors tried retraining models using downsampled balanced datasets and ensemble learning methods that combine predictions from multiple models.

I couldn't find the exact paper. The search returned no record of a "Leveraging Large Language Models for advanced static code analysis" article with the "superseding traditional vulnerability detection" phrasing, and nothing from *Information and Software Technology*. The results are related studies, though.

- **Benchmark comparisons:** A 2025 study of C# projects found that LLM-based scanners beat rule-based static tools on F1 score, mainly through higher recall ([Gnieciak and Szandala, arXiv:2508.04448](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.04448v1)). A separate summary of that work concludes that LLMs rival traditional analyzers but that their noisier output limits standalone use in audits ([Emergent Mind](https://api.emergentmind.com/papers/2508.04448)).
- **Hybrid approaches:** LSAST pairs static scanner output with LLM analysis and reports catching vulnerabilities that conventional tools miss ([arXiv:2409.15735](https://arxiv.org/html/2409.15735v2)). BugLens uses an LLM as a post-refinement step to raise the precision of existing static analyzers ([arXiv:2504.11711](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2504.11711)).
- **Off-the-shelf LLMs:** A Tallinn University benchmark compares prompting strategies and off-the-shelf LLMs against CodeQL and SpotBugs ([Tamberg, arXiv:2405.15614](https://arxiv.org/html/2405.15614v1)).

Overall, the literature supports LLMs as complements to static analysis, with recall gains but more false positives. None of these sources supports the claim that LLMs supersede traditional detection. If you need the *Information and Software Technology* paper specifically, search the journal on ScienceDirect or Scopus using the exact title.

input.old_string:
- **Statistics are rare.** Only tan2026think applies significance tests to its main comparison [@tan2026think, p. 6] [I, our count].
  - **Authors call for guidelines.** yildiz2025benchmarking calls for evaluation guidelines for JIT benchmarking [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 2] [A]. ding2025vulnerability proposes VD-S because accuracy and F1 mislead [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 2] [A].
- Novelty check (2026-11-12; Q4, Q5, Q9, Q10 on OpenAlex/arXiv from 2024/2025; W4). Closest hits:
  - *Pitfalls in Machine Learning for Computer Security* (CACM 2024, doi:10.1145/3643456) and *Pitfalls in LMs for Code Intelligence* (TOSEM 2025, doi:10.1145/3748647): generic pitfall catalogues with no re-scoring of vulnerability-detection results.
  - PrimeVul's VD-S and shu's dummy classifiers are in our corpus; each is applied only within its own study.
  - *How much model does warning triage need?* (American Impact Review 2026, doi:10.66308/air.e80134906): re-scores models against a simple reference with MCC and bootstrap CIs, but for actionable-warning triage, not vulnerability detection, and in an unknown-tier venue.
  - The CAI 2026 review (doi:10.70267/cai.v3n5.122137) recommends reporting practices but, from its abstract, does not recompute published results.

  We found no study that recomputes published LLM, SAST and DL vulnerability-detection results against trivial baselines and realistic prevalence (searches on 2026-11-12).
- Confidence: **medium–high**. The evidence comes from ≥6 independent primary studies. The only risk is an unpublished or non-indexed meta-analysis.
input.new_string:
- **Statistics are rare.** Among the first 16 primary studies, only tan2026think applies significance tests to its main comparison [@tan2026think, p. 6] [I, our count]. Of the four second-pass papers, deininger2026open uses a paired bootstrap with Holm correction [@deininger2026open, p. 6] [V].
  - **The decision rule and the prompt can flip conclusions.** At the default argmax threshold the fine-tuned PrimeVul detector predicts all-safe despite ROC-AUC 0.845; the authors nearly reported this as "trained detectors are no better than LLMs" [@deininger2026open, p. 11] [V]. Prompt paraphrases change the winning LLM [@deininger2026open, p. 20] [V].
  - **Authors call for guidelines.** yildiz2025benchmarking calls for evaluation guidelines for JIT benchmarking [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 2] [A]. ding2025vulnerability proposes VD-S because accuracy and F1 mislead [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 2] [A]. lu2025lab asks for cross-dataset and temporally separated testing plus patch-pair metrics [@lu2025lab, p. 16] [A].
- Novelty check (2026-11-12; first pass Q4, Q5, Q9, Q10 on OpenAlex/arXiv from 2024/2025 and W4; second pass Q35 on OpenAlex/Crossref from 2025). Closest work:

## G2: No same-benchmark, leakage-controlled comparison of LLMs vs SAST vs fine-tuned DL on real, post-cutoff code
- Gap type: evidence / methodological
- Evidence that the gap exists:
  - **Only one study runs all three families, and its SAST arm is synthetic.** khare2025understanding is the only study that evaluates LLMs, SAST and DL, and CodeQL runs on synthetic data only [@khare2025understanding, p. 7] [V].
  - **zhou2024comparison has no classic DL detector.** It compares fine-tuned and prompted LLMs with SAST [@zhou2024comparison, p. 4] [V].
input.new_string:
## G2: No same-benchmark, leakage-controlled comparison of LLMs vs semantic SAST vs fine-tuned DL on real, post-cutoff code with file or repository context
- Gap type: evidence / methodological
- **Second-pass verdict: narrowed.** deininger2026open fills the function-level, pre-cutoff, C/C++ version of this gap with lightweight SAST. What remains open: (a) post-cutoff targets, (b) file or repository context, (c) a semantic, build-based SAST arm such as CodeQL, and (d) a peer-reviewed non-C/C++ version (a function-level Python/Java/JS three-family preprint exists, abstract only; see novelty check).
- Evidence that the gap exists:
  - **Two studies in our corpus run all three families; each covers only part of the needed setting.**
    - khare2025understanding evaluates LLMs, SAST and DL, but CodeQL runs on synthetic data only [@khare2025understanding, p. 7] [V].
    - deininger2026open runs 8 zero-shot LLMs, Flawfinder 2.0.20, Cppcheck 2.21, Semgrep 1.175 and two CodeBERT detectors on the same 1549 PrimeVul C/C++ functions [@deininger2026open, p. 6; @deininger2026open, p. 10] [V]. Its limits are the ones that define what is left of G2:
      - CodeQL could not be run because the functions are unbuildable snippets [@deininger2026open, p. 10] [V];
      - all CVEs date from 2008–2022 and predate the models' training cutoffs, and recall is 7–15 points higher on pre-2020 CVEs [@deininger2026open, p. 24] [V];
      - function level, one dataset, C/C++ only [@deininger2026open, p. 25] [A];
      - the fine-tuned detector is in-distribution while the LLMs are zero-shot [@deininger2026open, p. 11] [A].
    - Its result shows why the gap still matters: the ranking depends on the metric. On balanced accuracy fine-tuned CodeBERT leads (0.765 vs ≤0.711 for LLMs); on precision at 1:44 prevalence Semgrep (26.0%, CI 5.7–66.9%) and strict Flawfinder (13.4%) lead, and every LLM is at 2.3–3.8% [@deininger2026open, p. 10; @deininger2026open, p. 17] [V].
  - **zhou2024comparison has no classic DL detector.** It compares fine-tuned and prompted LLMs with SAST [@zhou2024comparison, p. 4] [V].
  - **Temporal out-of-distribution evidence exists, but without SAST.** lu2025lab tests DL and four open LLMs on VentiVul, built from Linux and Chromium CVEs disclosed from 1 May 2025 [@lu2025lab, p. 4] [V]. LineVul falls from F1 91–94.5 in distribution [@lu2025lab, p. 12] to 4.39–6.87 on VentiVul, and all 8 DL configurations score 3.47–8.65 [@lu2025lab, p. 13] [V]. No static-analysis tool is evaluated [I]. The authors cannot fully exclude LLM contamination because pre-training cutoffs are unknown [@lu2025lab, p. 17] [A].
  - **PHP evidence exists, but without LLMs or a standard SAST tool.** tashenova2026real compares an in-house taint analyser with ML and LSTM detectors under plugin-grouped, de-duplicated folds [@tashenova2026real, p. 5] [V]; no LLM or transformer was run [@tashenova2026real, p. 13] [V].

                          2.3. The Gap
                               Cost has recently begun to appear in LLM security evaluations. Lira et al. assessed the
                          effectiveness and inference cost of four proprietary models on interprocedural vulnerability
                          detection over ReposVul [21], and other recent work has compared open and frontier
                          models on security detection tasks, including web vulnerability detection in WordPress
                          plugins [22] and dual-mode function- and application-level detection [23]. This is the
                          immediate context for our study, and it is moving quickly.
                               We, therefore, state our contribution as a specific combination rather than as a priority.
                          Table 1 compares this paper against the closest prior studies on three axes. Monetary cost is
                          now reported by some security evaluations; energy is reported by none of them, and the
                          general-purpose benchmarks that do treat energy seriously [5,7,17,20] do not evaluate a
                          security detection task. Breadth of open-weight coverage is likewise uneven: the study
                          that reports cost most carefully evaluates only proprietary models. What is new here is the
                          conjunction—a security detection task, a five-model open-weight roster spanning 4B to
                          671B total parameters, and cost and energy reported as co-equal per-task axes, with energy
                          measured directly where the model can be self-hosted. We make no claim to be first on any

## G6: No cost-per-confirmed-vulnerability comparison across LLM, SAST and DL including human triage effort
- Gap type: practical
- Evidence that the gap exists:
  - **Most studies report no monetary cost.** Ten of 16 primary studies report none [I, our count]. The six that do are du, guo, li2026llm, shu, tan and xiong [@du2026reducing, p. 8; @guo2025repoaudit, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 16; @shu2026evaluating, p. 42; @tan2026think, p. 10; @xiong2026sifting, p. 17].
  - **Where measured, cost is decisive.**
    - Per project: from $2.54 in the RepoAudit paper to $172.77 on average and $1,247.66 at most in li2026llm [@guo2025repoaudit, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 16] [V].
    - Thinking mode costs 2.7–4.4× the energy [@tan2026think, p. 10] [V].
  - **Cost is not linked to triage effort.** None of the cost figures is expressed per confirmed true positive, including the analyst time spent on false warnings [I]. li2026llm calls for cost-aware designs [@li2026llm, p. 18] [A].
- Novelty check (2026-11-12; Q15, Q16, Q25 on OpenAlex/arXiv/Crossref from 2024/2025; W7). Closest hits:
  - *Open or Frontier?* (Computers 2026, doi:10.3390/computers15090623): measures cost and energy for 8 LLMs vs a fine-tuned detector, with precision at 1:44 prevalence. **No SAST, no triage effort.** This narrows the gap considerably.
  - *Vulnerability Detection with Interprocedural Context in Multiple Languages* (arXiv 2604.08417): cost per LLM configuration only.
  - Vendor blogs (Semgrep, Endor Labs) report cost per true positive for their own products; these are not peer-reviewed and have conflicts of interest.

  We found no peer-reviewed study reporting cost per confirmed vulnerability, including triage time, for all three families on the same targets (searches on 2026-11-12).
- Confidence: **low–medium**. The gap is narrowed by *Open or Frontier?*. What remains is the SAST arm and the triage-effort term.
- Potential contribution: a decision-oriented metric for practitioners: dollars and analyst minutes per real vulnerability found.
- Suggested study: measure as a secondary outcome of G2 (same targets). Record compute cost per arm, then time two raters triaging a random 50 warnings per arm. Cost per TP = (compute + triage minutes × hourly rate) / confirmed TPs, reported with sensitivity bands for hourly rates. Threats: triage time depends on rater skill; API price changes.

## G6: No cost-per-confirmed-vulnerability comparison that includes human triage effort and a costed SAST and DL arm on the same targets
- Gap type: practical
- **Second-pass verdict: narrowed.** deininger2026open now reports compute cost (USD) and energy (kJ) per true positive at realistic prevalence for 8 LLMs. What remains open is (a) the human triage term, i.e. analyst time spent on the false positives that come with each true positive, and (b) a quantified cost per true positive for the SAST and fine-tuned DL arms on the same targets.
- Evidence that the gap exists:
  - **Most studies report no monetary cost.** 13 of our 20 primary studies report none [I, our count]. The seven that do are du, guo, li2026llm, shu, tan, xiong and deininger [@du2026reducing, p. 8; @guo2025repoaudit, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 16; @shu2026evaluating, p. 42; @tan2026think, p. 10; @xiong2026sifting, p. 17; @deininger2026open, p. 7].
  - **Where measured, cost is decisive.**
    - Per project: from $2.54 in the RepoAudit paper to $172.77 on average and $1,247.66 at most in li2026llm [@guo2025repoaudit, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 16] [V].
    - Thinking mode costs 2.7–4.4× the energy [@tan2026think, p. 10] [V]; in deininger2026open reasoning costs 4.5–12.1× more per task [@deininger2026open, p. 18] [V].
  - **Compute cost per true positive now exists for LLMs, but not for the other families and not for triage.**
    - deininger2026open reports USD 0.003 (Gemma-3-4B) to 0.212 (Claude-Sonnet-5) and 3.7 to 119.6 kJ per true positive at 1:44 prevalence [@deininger2026open, p. 8] [V].
    - Flawfinder is given as ≈0 cost per true positive [@deininger2026open, p. 8] [V]. No cost per true positive is quantified for CodeBERT ("negligible inference cost") or for Cppcheck and Semgrep [@deininger2026open, p. 8; @deininger2026open, p. 11] [V].
    - Each LLM true positive comes with 25.6–41.9 false positives [@deininger2026open, p. 8] [V]. The paper notes that no triage workflow absorbs that alert volume [@deininger2026open, p. 8], but analyst time is not costed [I]. At such ratios analyst time would plausibly dominate compute cost of a few cents per true positive [I].
    - Caveat for anyone reusing Table 5: its kJ per true positive for Qwen3-Coder-30B (4.0) and Llama-3.3-70B (44.8) uses FLOP estimates, not the measured per-task energy (88 J and 738 J) [@deininger2026open, p. 7; @deininger2026open, p. 8; @deininger2026open, p. 14] [V]. Recomputed from the measured values these are about 8.8 and 34.9 kJ per true positive [I, from critical review D].
  - **Calls for audit-time measurement.** li2026llm calls for cost-aware designs [@li2026llm, p. 18] [A]. qin2026review recommends human-machine studies that record audit time per real vulnerability, and SAST-LLM systems evaluated by total audit cost [@qin2026review, p. 13] [A] (narrative review; not independent evidence).
- Novelty check (2026-11-12; first pass Q15, Q16, Q25 on OpenAlex/arXiv/Crossref from 2024/2025 and W7; second pass Q30 on OpenAlex/Crossref and Q31 on OpenAlex, both from 2025, and W11). Closest work:
  - **deininger2026open** (in corpus; see evidence above): compute cost and energy per true positive for LLMs; no triage term; SAST and DL arms not costed per true positive.
  - deininger2026open's related-work table rates Neef et al. (arXiv 2606.21397) and Dahiya et al. (arXiv 2605.23243) as giving partial treatment of cost [@deininger2026open, p. 3] [A]. Neither abstract mentions cost, a SAST arm or triage time (A1, A2; abstract only).
  - *Vulnerability Detection with Interprocedural Context in Multiple Languages* (arXiv 2604.08417): cost per LLM configuration only.
  - *Demystifying the Mythos or Disrupting Bugonomics?* (arXiv 2605.24632, preprint; abstract only, W11): argues qualitatively that validation and triage capacity, not bug finding, is the bottleneck; the abstract reports no measured triage time and no cost per vulnerability.
  - Grey literature (W11; not peer-reviewed): vendor benchmarks (Semgrep, June 2026) report dollars per true positive for their own products, and a practitioner write-up of an LLM-assisted audit reports API cost per confirmed finding *before* human validation. Both have conflicts of interest or no peer review, and neither includes analyst time.

  We found no peer-reviewed study reporting cost per confirmed vulnerability that includes human triage time, for LLM, SAST and DL arms on the same targets (searches on 2026-11-12).
- Confidence: **low–medium** (narrowed). What remains is specific (triage term plus costed non-LLM arms) and fits as a secondary outcome of G2.
- Potential contribution: a decision-oriented metric for practitioners: dollars and analyst minutes per real vulnerability found. It would extend deininger2026open's compute-only USD per true positive with the term that probably dominates it [I].
- Suggested study: measure as a secondary outcome of G2 (same targets). Record compute cost per arm (for SAST and DL: CPU/GPU time × a stated hourly rate, so that they are not left at "≈0"), then time two raters triaging a random 50 warnings per arm. Cost per confirmed TP = (compute + triage minutes × hourly rate) / confirmed TPs, reported with sensitivity bands for hourly rates and at realistic prevalence (e.g. 1:44 as in deininger2026open). Use measured, not FLOP-estimated, energy where possible. Threats: triage time depends on rater skill and on the order in which warnings are shown; API price changes and provider price spread (up to 14× for one model [@deininger2026open, p. 5]).

I've updated the gap report in place, with the existing structure kept. `rlab cite-check` passes: 171 citations covering 24 papers. G2, G5 and G6 are narrowed, G1, G3 and G4 are unchanged, none closes and there is no new gap.

File: /Users/makky/Downloads/AI-Research-Lab-main/research/2026-11-12-llm-based-vs-traditional-static-analysis/gap-report.md

**One omission from the first pass.** arXiv 2503.01449 (Zhang et al. 2025, abstract only) compares five open LLMs, five fine-tuned small models and two open-source static analysis (SAST) tools on the same function-level data in Python, Java and JS. The first-pass search Q17 returned it, but the first report never mentioned it. It is now recorded under G2 and G5 and is the top new paper to add.

## Per-gap verdicts
- **G1, unchanged (medium–high).** Trivial baselines are now reported or derivable in shu, deininger and tashenova, with lu's chance level derivable (7 of its 12 LLM F1 values fall below the 3.87% all-positive level). Each applies the baseline only to its own results, so a systematic re-scoring across studies is still open. The contribution is now framed as "cross-study" and credits these within-study baselines. Q35 found nothing relevant.
- **G2, narrowed (medium).** deininger2026open already compares LLMs, lightweight SAST and DL on the same pre-cutoff C/C++ functions. What remains:
  - code disclosed after the models' training cutoffs;
  - file or repository context;
  - a semantic SAST tool that needs a build, such as CodeQL;
  - a peer-reviewed version outside C/C++ (2503.01449 partly covers this, abstract only).
  
  lu2025lab's post-May-2025 evidence is added; the "No SAST" note is corrected; and the low-cost study variant now reuses lu2025lab's public VentiVul set.
- **G3, unchanged (low–medium).** None of the new papers studies LLM filtering of SAST alarms.
- **G4, unchanged (medium).** None of the new papers studies hybrid LLM+SAST tools.
- **G5, narrowed (low–medium).** It is now: real-CVE comparisons of LLMs against established SAST tools in PHP and Go. Neef et al. covers LLMs on real WordPress plugins without a SAST arm (abstract only). tashenova is now cited from full text: its "misses ~98%" result comes from an unnamed in-house analyser and it has no LLM. The study now uses tashenova's released 125 vulnerable / 247 safe expert-verified subset.
- **G6, narrowed (low–medium).** deininger reports compute cost and energy per true positive for 8 LLMs. Still missing: analyst triage time (25.6–41.9 false positives come with each true positive) and a cost figure for the SAST and DL arms. I added the caveat that Table 5's kJ figures for Qwen and Llama use estimates, not the measured values (about 8.8 and 34.9 kJ when recomputed). qin2026review is cited only as a call for audit-time studies.
- **Positioning.** qin2026review is the CAI 2026 review, so it moved into the in-corpus table. It shares our framing, but it is narrative, has no search protocol, leaves SAST out of scope (p. 4) and relies on ding, gnieciak and sheng (p. 15). It supports our novelty claim but is not independent evidence. The corpus count is updated to 24 papers (20 primary studies).

## Novelty checks (all 2026-11-12, recorded in the log)
- **A1, Neef et al. (arXiv 2606.21397; AI&CCPS @ ARES 2026, doi:10.1007/978-3-032-35576-8_3), abstract only.**
  - Six frontier and open LLMs on real WordPress-plugin vulnerabilities (SQL injection, stored XSS, path traversal, RCE), with five prompt designs and three runs. Best detection rate is 63% (Claude Opus 4.6).
  - The abstract names no SAST baseline and no DL detector, and does not give the plugin or CVE count or the input granularity.
  - deininger's p. 3 table rates it as partly reporting cost.
  - Verdict: G5 narrowed, not closed. The full text needs checking for a tool baseline and repository-level input.
- **A2, Dahiya et al. (arXiv 2605.23243, v5), abstract only.** Function-level C/Java/Python (on VulnLLM-R), plus black-box testing of 5 web apps (118 vulnerabilities). No SAST, no DL baseline, no temporal control, and its application-level track is black-box testing rather than source analysis. Verdict: does not fill G2.
- **New searches Q27–Q35 (from 2025, OpenAlex/Crossref, Q34 on arXiv) and WebSearches W9–W12.** The arXiv API timed out on 6 queries, which is noted in the log; the two arXiv papers were checked through their abstract pages.
  - No 2026 study runs all three families on the same post-cutoff code with context.
  - No peer-reviewed cost-per-confirmed-vulnerability study includes triage time. Only vendor or grey sources (Semgrep's June 2026 blog, a practitioner write-up) and arXiv 2605.24632 exist; the last is qualitative and abstract only.

## Recommended for inclusion (not analysed)
1. arXiv 2503.01449, Zhang et al. 2025, multi-language three-family benchmark (preprint). High priority.
2. arXiv 2606.21397 / doi:10.1007/978-3-032-35576-8_3, Neef et al. 2026. Closest work to G5.
3. doi:10.1016/j.infsof.2026.108213, Information and Software Technology 2026, "Leveraging LLMs for advanced static code analysis…". Title only (no abstract found), so screen it first.
4. arXiv 2605.23243, Dahiya et al. 2026. Low priority.
5. Optional: doi:10.66571/tsarka-3134-6057-11 (TSARKA 2026, web snippets, compares LLMs with an all-vulnerable baseline; venue tier unknown).

Still on the list from the first pass: doi:10.5070/sr3.62177, arXiv 2604.13764, and the optional 2510.02534, 2610.32876 and 2507.21817. The first-pass items 1–4 are removed because they are now in the corpus.

## Left for you
I did not run `rlab index` or `rlab log` because the orchestrator owns those. I also did not edit STATUS.md.
